removed: top of page Home Meet Priorities News Newsletters Events Help Donate Week 31: Being Available to Meet Everyone Celeste Landry Sep 15 2 min read Updated: Sep 19 Dear Colorado Voter, You’ve probably heard by now that Colorado’s mail ballots may proceed as usual.
The Supreme Court ruled that the U.S.
Postal Service may NOT change mail-ballot procedures this year.

Justices Alito and Thomas dissented, while Justice Kavanaugh thought the USPS argument had merit but concurred with the majority that “officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before” the November 2026 election.
As a candidate, my life continues to proceed unusually.
As I said in the Sept 10th Meet the Forwardists online event with Chuck Todd, a statewide candidate has a special pass to meet VIPs, and that has been fun!
Brian Bengs called my home, and we chatted about our respective campaigns.
Bengs is an independent U.S.
Senate candidate in South Dakota giving the incumbent a run for his money!
Bengs had to collect 3,502 signatures, the Republican 2,171, the Democrat 1,232 and any Libertarian 741.

If I had not gotten ballot access via the Forward Party, I would have had to collect more than 8,000 signatures – at least 1,000 from each congressional district – but any major-party Secretary of State candidate petitioning onto the Colorado ballot would have had the same signature requirements.

(You can read on my website’s Priorities page about the lowered signature requirements for county offices that my friend Britta and I got into the 2019 omnibus elections bill, HB19-1278.) During this campaign, I’ve enjoyed going to events which span the political spectrum.
I’ve long appreciated hearing differing opinions and believe people in public service have a duty to try to show up when invited.

(By the way, I won’t be at the Club 20 debate in Grand Junction this coming weekend because only the Democrat and Republican were invited.) “Holding regular constituent engagement sessions” is part of the Forward Party candidate pledge.
My weekly online Ask Me Anything sessions are on different days and times for better accessibility – see my website.
As Secretary of State, I’d like to continue holding weekly online public sessions.
I believe that regular communication is an antidote to polarization.
Ronald Reagan and Tip O’Neill were fierce opponents during the day, but famously on friendly terms after 6pm.
These days tribalism in the U.S. means opponents are enemies 24/7.
How can a government function if it’s always one side versus the other instead of working for what’s best for all of us?
Let’s come together!
With enthusiasm and purpose, Celeste Celeste Landry for Secretary of State P.O.

title.after: Week 35: The "mass media" campaign

added: top of page Home Meet Priorities News Newsletters Events Help Donate Week 35: The "mass media" campaign Celeste Landry #ago 2 min read Dear Colorado Voter, It’s been a busy week!

Wed, Oct 7 – City Matters* podcast out of CO Springs https://open.spotify.com/episode/1WaDgyYrsKIYGccXh98iFy Thurs, Oct 8 – New campaign literature* now prominently posted on my website’s home page Fri, Oct 9 – Kalshi https://kalshi.com/markets/kxsecstateco/co-secstate/kxsecstateco-26 Sat, Oct 10 – Colorado Politics’ only-major-party-candidates debate.
My supporters and I showed up to tell the world that I’m a candidate and was being excluded by a news outlet!

Sat, Oct 10 and Sun, Oct 11 – Colorado Point of View* https://youtu.be/- v1aLmRjz60?t=790 Mon, Oct 12 – Billboard ~1 mile north of S Academy Blvd exit #135 Tues, Oct 13 – Kim Monson Show* KLZ 560 Denver https://kimmonson.com/kim_monson_show/amendment-83-proposition134-girls-sports-governor-race-vacancy-elections/ Tues, Oct 13 – letter to the Daily Camera editor https://www.dailycamera.com/2026/10/13/dirty-tactics-advance-coloradoamendment-82-election/ Excerpt: The Camera truly buried the lede in its article on the Secretary of State race (Oct.
Under the headline“Candidates looking to depoliticize the office,”the article focused on the two candidates from the two major parties.
There were only a few words about Celeste Landry.

Celeste has made removing partisanship from running Colorado’s elections her central campaign theme, very much “depoliticizing the office.” A common theme of the asterisked items is my commitment to protect Coloradans’ right to vote.

Unfortunately, this right can no longer be taken for granted after the CO state legislature passed two party-protection bills that disenfranchise registered voters who belong to the “wrong” party in oddyear special vacancy elections.
November 2025 voters in El Paso County Commissioner District 5 only saw the county commissioner contest on their ballot if they were Republican or unaffiliated!
In November 2027 vacancies in the state legislature are scheduled to be filled in party-protection elections – but not if I’m elected Secretary of State!
After swearing an oath to the U.S. and CO Constitutions, I will not conduct these unconstitutional elections.
I wish that a news outlet would ask the other SoS candidates what they think about these party-protection bills.
I want them on the record!
My Democratic opponent didn’t have time to talk to me about the partyprotection elections before or after the Saturday debate.
My Republican opponent indicated to me that he would probably refuse to conduct these unconstitutional elections.
Bob Chew (U.S.
Senate), Greg Lopez (Governor), and I are running active, credible campaigns and offering voters an option besides the two major parties.
When you mark your ballot, please give the three of us statewide candidates as much consideration as you give the major-party candidates.
With enthusiasm and purpose, Celeste Celeste Landry for Secretary of State P.O.

top of page Home Meet Priorities News Newsletters Events Help Donate Week 22: Why is Celeste running?
Celeste Landry Jul 14 2 min read Updated: Sep 13 Dear Colorado Voter, I'm sometimes asked, "Why are you running for Secretary of State?" 1.
I have the experience, vision, and leadership qualities to be a great Secretary of State.

For about a decade, I have worked with the office and legislators to make Colorado's elections and election laws the best in the nation, often as a member of the nonpartisan League of Women Voters (LWV).
Two bills passed in 2025 that, for the first time in American history, disenfranchise voters based on party affiliation in government-run special elections.
The other SoS candidates do not appear concerned about these clearly unconstitutional, party-protection bills.
I led an LWV effort to challenge these bills and proposed a better, constitutional option in a January 2024 Colorado Sun guest opinion .
Proportional representation is the best way to end gerrymandering and ensure that a spectrum of voices reflective of the electorate can serve on governmental bodies.
In 2018 I introduced then-candidate Joe Neguse to the U.S.
Fair Representation Act, which calls for electing congressional delegations using a proportional voting method.
Congressman Neguse has been a bill co-sponsor ever since.
Meanwhile, several communities are waiting for the CO SoS to fulfill their statutory duty and write rules for county clerks to conduct a proportional-voting election.

When voters are limited to choose-one voting, candidates often effectively resort to negative campaigning, and vote-splitting between 2 or more candidates can result in electing the candidate with the least support.
Approval Voting is a simple voting method that addresses these problems and can be implemented quickly – St.
Louis did it in 4 months – if the SoS writes implementation rules, which I would do.
The Forward Party is about as non-partisan as a party can be.
Its platform is perfect for county clerks and secretaries of state.
Most voters in Colorado are unaffiliated.
In our politically polarized world, my candidacy as neither a D nor an R gives Colorado a chance to break out of the mold of political people running elections.
I see a path to victory if I can get out the word about my candidacy.
I will defend your right to vote, facilitate implementation of better voting methods so you can have better representation, and protect our elections.
You can help by asking the media to cover my campaign and by introducing me to CO voters.
Then I'll "be ready when the luck happens!" With enthusiasm and purpose, Celeste Celeste Landry for Secretary of State P.O.

It is very interesting.
Usually non-significant or tiny numbers will be classified as “others”, not the second largest numbers.
“Others” here refers to “Asian American”.
After pulling some data after 2011, I did not see student enrollment is decreasing, instead it is stabilizing around 1300.
At the same time, we should look at the enrollment number in the elementary schools and middle schools nearby, which may show us some trend.
I will look at those numbers later.

The victim’s family want to attended their son’s funeral and the US consular denied their visa application.
Just read how the visa application was denied in five seconds, the process sometimes is inhumane and unbelievable wrong.
Our state senate Susan Lee called me back and offered to help.
I really appreciate her effort.
Dear our elected Asian American Caucus, (Their email is aapicaucus@senate.state.md.us ) We need your urgent help for a visa application.
There was a triple murder in Bowie, Maryland in January.
The news is here: http://wtop.com/prince-georges-county/2017/01/police-id-3-victims-in-homicide-at-bowie-restaurant/ I just heard that the victim’s family members of Mr.
Jin Chen in China applied for visa to attend the funeral in Maryland and were denied the visa.
They were thinking of applying for the visa again on this Friday (Feb 24) at the US consular at Guangzhou, China.
It was reported that Chen’s family member was asked a question whether Mr.
Chen was married.
After the family member replied with a “yes”, then the visa application was denied immediately.
I just could not think of a situation like this.
A visa to attend a family funeral in a terrible murder case was denied without any sound reasons.
Can any of you do something to help their family members to get a visa?
You can write to the state department and the US consular at Guangzhou, China to express your support to grant a visa to Mr.
Chen’s family member.
Such kind of letters usually help.
Thank you very much.
Dr.

Chao Wu A resident from Howard County, Maryland Share this: Share Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Like this: Like Loading… Related Post navigation ← → 2 thoughts on “ Inhumane and unbelievable of US visa application ” Andrew says: I am sorry to hear the story.

As you may know, certain reagions in China have produced tens of thousand of illegal immigrants, and they applied political asylum, such as forced family planning and other excuses to obtain PR, then come back and forth between China and the US.
These patterns have caused alarms in US counselors.
It is plausible that he had married and had a wife and several family members in the US.
It is regretable that his extended family could not come, but the US counsulor could use his or her discretion to deny the visas.

It aims to expose high school students to the applications of a STEM-based education as well as the various internship opportunities offered by well-known organizations (NIH, NSA, JHU, UMD).
The format includes a keynote presentation, 2 workshop sessions, and a booths fair.
You can register for the conference through this form, but note that it will close on November 29th and will be limited to the first 300 entries.

title.after: Southern Nevada Community Q&A | English & Español

added: COMMUNITY INFORMATION · INFORMACIÓN PARA LA COMUNIDAD Questions that affect everyday life Preguntas que afectan la vida cotidiana A nonpartisan guide for Southern Nevada residents.
Current developments, upcoming changes and practical resources.
Una guía no partidista para residentes del sur de Nevada.
Acontecimientos actuales, próximos cambios y recursos prácticos.
Information checked / Información verificada: October 12, 2026 · 12 de octubre de 2026 English Español English Upcoming · January 2027 1.
Who faces new Nevada Medicaid requirements?
Nevada says some members will need to work, volunteer, or attend school beginning January 1, 2027.
Exemptions include certain parents, pregnant people, people with disabilities or serious health conditions, and people age 65 or older.
Update your contact information and check your renewal date.
Ask the state whether an exemption applies; do not assume every member faces these rules.
Source: Nevada Division of Social Services Available now · enrollment ahead 2.
What can families do now about health insurance for next year?
Nevada Health Link says next-year plans can be previewed starting October 1; enrollment begins November 1.
Compare premiums, deductibles, prescriptions and provider networks.
Update income and household information.
Free enrollment assistance is available at 1-800-547-2927.
Confirm the closing date directly: retrieved official pages contain differing deadlines for the upcoming enrollment period.
Source: Nevada Health Link Announced · effective October 16, 2026 3.
What immigration change takes effect this week?
USCIS announced inflation increases for certain immigration-related fees, effective October 16.
For example, the specified initial asylum, parole and TPS employment authorization fee rises from $560 to $570; the TPS application fee rises from $510 to $520.
These are specified fees, not necessarily the full cost of a filing.
Check the current fee schedule and instructions for your exact application before submitting it.
Source: USCIS bulletin · September 30, 2026 Upcoming · 2027 drug costs 4.
What Medicare drug costs are changing?
The Part D out-of-pocket limit for covered drugs increases from $2,100 in 2026 to $2,400 in 2027.
Premiums and noncovered drugs are outside this limit.
The maximum deductible rises from $615 to $700; some plans charge less or no deductible.
Compare your own plan.
The prescription payment option spreads costs across the year but does not reduce them.
Source: Medicare.gov Current rules · wages 5.
What is Nevada’s minimum wage, and where can workers ask for help?
Nevada’s minimum wage is $12 per hour, effective since July 1, 2024.
The state Labor Commissioner accepts wage complaints and provides information about overtime and other workplace rules.
Keep pay statements and records of hours worked.
Rules and exemptions vary; contact the Las Vegas office at 702-486-2650 about your situation.
Source: Nevada Office of the Labor Commissioner Program operating in 2026 6.
Is help available for a renter facing eviction?
Legal Aid describes an eviction diversion program beginning February 2, 2026, for eligible renters age 62 or older and people receiving SSI because of disability.
It covers specified nonpayment cases in Las Vegas, Henderson and North Las Vegas.
A timely tenant answer is required.
Rental assistance depends on eligibility and availability; it is not guaranteed.
Other tenants can ask Legal Aid about available help.
Source: Legal Aid Center of Southern Nevada Existing resource · small businesses 7.
Where can small business owners get practical help?
The Small Business Administration and its resource partners offer free or low-cost counseling and training.
Use the local assistance directory to find help with business planning and financing questions.
Counseling does not guarantee approval for a loan or grant.
Source: U.S.
Small Business Administration What could lawmakers consider?
Possible legislative approaches include simpler benefit notices and appeals, funding for affordable housing, enforcement of wage laws, and changes to immigration processing capacity or fees.
These are policy options for public discussion, not claims that a bill has been introduced or enacted.
Each would need a defined scope, funding, and evaluation of costs and benefits.
Federal lawmakers, state lawmakers and local governments have different responsibilities.
Español Próximamente · enero de 2027 1. ¿A quiénes afectan los nuevos requisitos de Medicaid en Nevada?
Nevada informa que algunos miembros deberán trabajar, hacer voluntariado o estudiar a partir del 1 de enero de 2027.
Hay excepciones para ciertos padres, personas embarazadas, personas con discapacidades o enfermedades graves y personas de 65 años o más.
Actualice sus datos de contacto y revise su fecha de renovación.
Consulte al estado si tiene una excepción; las reglas no afectan a todos.
Fuente: Nevada Division of Social Services Disponible ahora · próxima inscripción 2. ¿Qué pueden hacer las familias ahora sobre el seguro médico del próximo año?
Nevada Health Link permite consultar los planes del próximo año desde el 1 de octubre; la inscripción comienza el 1 de noviembre.
Compare primas, deducibles, medicamentos y redes de proveedores.
Actualice ingresos y datos del hogar.
Hay ayuda gratuita en el 1-800-547-2927.
Confirme directamente la fecha de cierre: las páginas oficiales consultadas muestran fechas distintas para el próximo período.
Fuente: Nevada Health Link Anunciado · vigente desde el 16 de octubre de 2026 3. ¿Qué cambio migratorio entra en vigor esta semana?
USCIS anunció aumentos por inflación en ciertas tarifas migratorias, vigentes desde el 16 de octubre.
Por ejemplo, la tarifa indicada para el permiso inicial de trabajo por asilo, permiso humanitario o TPS sube de $560 a $570; la solicitud de TPS sube de $510 a $520.
Estas tarifas no necesariamente representan el costo total del trámite.
Revise las tarifas e instrucciones actuales para su solicitud antes de enviarla.
Fuente: USCIS bulletin · September 30, 2026 Próximamente · medicamentos en 2027 4. ¿Qué costos de medicamentos de Medicare cambian?
El límite de gastos de bolsillo de la Parte D para medicamentos cubiertos sube de $2,100 en 2026 a $2,400 en 2027.
Las primas y medicamentos no cubiertos quedan fuera del límite.
El deducible máximo sube de $615 a $700; algunos planes cobran menos o ninguno.
Compare su propio plan.
La opción de pagos de medicamentos distribuye los gastos durante el año, pero no los reduce.
Fuente: Medicare.gov Reglas actuales · salarios 5. ¿Cuál es el salario mínimo de Nevada y dónde pueden pedir ayuda los trabajadores?
El salario mínimo de Nevada es de $12 por hora desde el 1 de julio de 2024.
El Comisionado Laboral recibe reclamos salariales e informa sobre horas extra y otras reglas laborales.
Guarde comprobantes de pago y registros de horas trabajadas.
Las reglas y excepciones varían; consulte su situación con la oficina de Las Vegas en el 702-486-2650.
Fuente: Nevada Office of the Labor Commissioner Programa disponible en 2026 6. ¿Hay ayuda para un inquilino que enfrenta un desalojo?
Legal Aid describe un programa de prevención de desalojos iniciado el 2 de febrero de 2026 para inquilinos elegibles de 62 años o más y personas que reciben SSI por discapacidad.
Abarca ciertos casos de falta de pago en Las Vegas, Henderson y North Las Vegas.
Debe presentar su respuesta dentro del plazo.
La ayuda depende de elegibilidad y disponibilidad; no está garantizada.
Otros inquilinos pueden consultar qué ayuda existe.
Fuente: Legal Aid Center of Southern Nevada Recurso existente · pequeñas empresas 7. ¿Dónde pueden obtener ayuda práctica los pequeños empresarios?
La Administración de Pequeñas Empresas (SBA) y sus organizaciones colaboradoras ofrecen asesoría y capacitación gratuitas o de bajo costo.
Use el directorio local para buscar ayuda con planes de negocio y financiamiento.
La asesoría no garantiza la aprobación de un préstamo o subvención.
Fuente: U.S.
Small Business Administration ¿Qué podrían considerar los legisladores?

Entre las opciones están avisos y apelaciones de beneficios más sencillos, fondos para vivienda asequible, cumplimiento de leyes salariales y cambios en la capacidad de procesamiento o tarifas migratorias.
Son opciones para debate público; no se afirma que exista un proyecto presentado o una ley aprobada.
Cada opción requiere definir su alcance, financiamiento, costos y beneficios.
Los gobiernos federal, estatal y local tienen responsabilidades distintas.
Rules, court orders and program availability can change.
Follow the linked agency’s current instructions for your individual situation.
No personal information is collected on this page.
Las reglas, órdenes judiciales y disponibilidad de programas pueden cambiar.
Siga las instrucciones actuales de la agencia para su caso particular.
Esta página no recopila información personal.

All Articles Environmental Activism Equality Issues Search Jun 10, 2020 1 min read Updated: Sep 9, 2020 We're creating a new hemp industry in Hawaii.
The Governor just signed our bill I cosponsored into law.
HB1819 legalizes the growing, processing, and sale of industrial hemp in Hawai‘i.
Hemp is an amazing crop that can create over 25,000 products.
This big step forward will help local farmers develop a new cottage industry with Hawai‘i branding that can be recognized and exported.
It will help diversify and expand our economy, especially now in the midst of this crisis.
We're going to have a lot more work to do to help small farmers lead the way and compete with their own brands, but this is a big first step.
This was me, Representative Cynthia Theilen, and Senator Laura Thielen breaking ground to help plant the very first hemp seeds in Waimanalo.
The incredible success of this pilot project helped lead to the passage of this bill, and will lead to incredible new opportunities for local farmers in the months and years to come.
HB1819 was signed into law as Act 14 on August 27.

“Gas is over four dollars a gallon in New Hampshire because of Donald Trump’s reckless war with Iran which John Sununu supports and is profiting from,” said Chris Pappas for Senate spokesperson Gates MacPherson .

The votes cited in the ad were Senate roll call votes, including on days the House of Representatives was not in session.
The House was not in session on 8/10/21, 3/6/21, or 8/7/22.

Congressman Pappas is Fighting to Lower Energy Costs And Increase Energy Independence Congressman Pappas voted for legislation to advance energy independence while lowering costs for New Hampshire families.
Congressman Pappas repeatedly broke with Democrats to combat overly burdensome energy efficiency rules and to speed up energy production.

Congressman Pappas is leading efforts to suspend the federal gas tax to provide Granite Staters with relief at the pump and hold oil companies accountable if they fail to pass savings along to consumers.
Congressman Pappas is pushing for bipartisan energy tax cuts for the middle class.
Congressman Pappas is working to lower utility bills for veterans and military families .
Congressman Pappas is fighting to protect thousands of families who rely on LIHEAP to heat and cool their homes.
John Sununu is Profiting From Trump’s War With Iran While Granite Staters Pay More at the Pump John Sununu is getting richer off Trump’s war with Iran due to his investments in oil and gas companies.
John Sununu reported owning between $77,000 and $280,000 in gas and oil stock, including up to $50,000 in ExxonMobil and $65,000 in Shell.
John Sununu’s oil and gas portfolio has grown by 24% since November 2025, with the biggest spikes following the January incursion into Venezuela and the February bombing of Iran .

John Sununu backs Trump’s war with Iran and downplayed the impact on higher gas prices, saying, “ I think it’s a step in the right direction. ” The average price of gas in New Hampshire is $4.35 , up from about $2.90 #ago.

A new survey from the University of New Hampshire found that 61% of New Hampshire residents are worried about paying for gas over the next 12 months, and 42% said they have cut spending on non-essentials and are driving less in their day-to-day life because of the high prices.

Senate Debates October 15, 2026 MANCHESTER, N.H. — After debate-dodging his way through the Republican primary, it’s no wonder Sununu’s rusty.

Through two debates against Chris Pappas, John Sununu has done nothing to convince voters that he will be more than a rubber stamp for Donald Trump, living up to his pledge that his race is “ important to President Trump’s agenda .” Accumulating a record over the course of the campaign of supporting and downplaying the worst parts of President Trump’s agenda — including Trump’s war with Iran , Trump’s tariff taxes , and Trump’s cuts to health care — Sununu has now embarrassed himself on stage repeatedly: Defending his plan to privatize Social Security, refusing to pledge to vote for Iran War Powers Resolutions to end that war, and even standing up for Pete Hegseth against pushes for accountability.

Read and watch key lowlights from the first two debates below: Sununu Touted His Record of Privatizing Social Security and Explicitly Told Voters He’s Hiding What He’ll Do If Elected When asked how he would address future shortcomings in the Social Security trust fund, Sununu initially refused to lay out what specific changes he would support before going back to his repeated attempts to privatize Social Security while in office.

WATCH : Sununu Tells the Moderator, “I’m Not Going to Lay Out Specific Changes [to Social Security] That I Support” WATCH : Sununu Touts his Repeated Attempts to Privatize Social Security in Office That Would’ve Exposed Granite Staters’ Retirement Accounts to Stock Market Crashes WATCH : Sununu Then Doubles Down by Touting his Privatization Plans Again During the Following Debate Sununu Refused to Support War Powers Resolution John Sununu, who has personally profited from the Iran War, specifically said that he opposes ending funding for the War right now, and has gone to great lengths at both debates now to refuse to support a War Powers Resolution, even when pushed directly on it.

WATCH : Sununu Says Regarding War “I Don’t Think it Would be Wise Right Now to Cut Off Funding” WATCH : Pappas Directly Pushes “Senator Sununu Hasn’t… Been Willing to Say That he Would Support a War Powers Resolution to Stop Donald Trump’s War Effort and to Bring our Troops Home” Sununu Refused to “Litigate” Whether he Would’ve Voted to Confirm Pete Hegseth, RFK Jr., or Kristi Noem Then Defends Hegseth Against Accountability Pushes the Next Night Trump lackey John Sununu was directly asked during the first debate if he would have supported Pete Hegseth, Robert F.
Kennedy Jr., and Kristi Noem, and he refused to say how he would vote on their nominations.

Even worse, the next night, Sununu went on a bizarre defense of Hegseth, saying that he should not be impeached despite Hegseth’s outrageous public failures and decisions to undermine our national security.

WATCH : Sununu Said, “I’m Not Going to Litigate Each” Confirmation Vote for Pete Hegseth, RFK Jr., or Kristi Noem WATCH : Sununu Passed on Voting to Impeach Pete Hegseth, Claiming, “You Shouldn’t be Impeached for a Bad Decision” Another Debate Moderator Mistook Sununu for his More Popular, More Charismatic, Little Brother A second debate moderator confused John Sununu with his younger, more charismatic brother Chris during the debate, before noting Chris is “definitely” not John when correcting himself.
Sununu’s yard signs still do not show his first name.

WATCH : Moderator Misidentifies Sununu as His Brother Ultimately, the Contrast in this Race Was Best Summed Up By Chris Pappas At the end of the day, Chris Pappas made the strongest case for why John Sununu’s new debate persona of “independence” wasn’t fooling anyone: WATCH : Pappas Eviscerated Sununu’s Record of Failing Granite Staters ### Join Team Pappas Sign up here to learn more about Chris, our campaign, and how you can get involved.

Home Candidate Issues Endorsements Come along Home Candidate Issues Endorsements Come along Get Involved Request a Yard Sign CLICK August 11 - October 28, 2026 DEADLINE TO FILL OUT ABSENTEE APPLICATION A Stronger Voice for District 10.

I’m running for the West Virginia House of Delegates because I believe in listening to our local communities, standing up for working families, supporting strong public services, and building responsible growth for today and for a better tomorrow in West Virginia.

CHRISTOPHER JONES WV HOUSE OF DELEGATES - DISTRICT 10 October 21 - October 31, 2026 EARLY VOTING Election Day Tuesday, November 3 2026 About the candidate : Christopher Jones is a husband, a father of 2, a community volunteer, youth soccer coach, Navy Veteran, and a life long West Virginia resident.
While being medically discharged from the Navy, and within the same week losing his federal government job, he came home wondering what was next.
His passion for service to the public pushed him into running for WV House District 10.
Rooted in Our Community.
Ready to serve.
What I’m Fighting For Real solutions to our schools, our communities and our future.
1st Issue Prioritizing Public Education Focusing on the need to fund public schools and protect the separation of church and state within our public schools.
2nd Issue Healthcare Fight against rising healthcare costs, and protecting access to preventative and reproductive healthcare.
3rd Issue Affordability Supporting practical policies that help lower everyday costs, expand access to affordable housing, fight to make PSC an elected seat.
4th Issue Fight for dependable utilities, safe drinking water, and investments to roads and towns for long term success.
5th Issue Infrustructure Infrustructure 6th Issue Workers’ Rights Supporting the right to organize, prevailing wage, safe workplaces, and opposing right to work.
7th Issue Veteran’s Benefits Continued fighting for the health of our Veterans and benefits they deserve Data Centers Oppose HB 2014 ; fight for the public’s input and environmental protections.
8th Issue Expand Energy Access Investing in clean, renewable energy sources and protecting future jobs for the coal industry DONATE!
Without monetary support, this campaign can’t purchase necessary items to connect to everyone within District 10!
COME ALONG FOR THE RIDE.
Join us!
Taking District 10 won’t be easy.
But with your help and support, we can win this seat and make meaningful change at the capitol!
FOLLOW US ON FB.
SHARE OUR PROFILE!
See whats happening real time as we trek through the campaign trail!
SIGN UP TO VOLUNTEER!
Making calls.
Knocking doors.
Showing our community we can rally behind candidates!
ElectJonesWV @gmail.com 304-991-0387 CONTACT US : Register to Check registration!
Find polling location!
CLICK CLICK See your sample ballot! vote!
ENDORSEMENTS I’m proud to have the support of local organization, unions, and community leaders who believe in a stronger, fairer West Virginia.
Their endorsements mean a lot, and I’m grateful for their trust.
WV Building & Construction Trades Plumbers & Steamfitters Local 565 EAS Carpenters Conservation WV WV Can’t Wait!
Planned Parenthood Votes South Atlantic INDIVISIBLEMOV Parkersburg-Marietta Construction Trades Council CLICK A STRONG VOICE FOR DISTRICT 10!
PUTTING OUR PEOPLE BEFORE POLITICS!

DONATE GET INVOLVED Join Christy, Sign Up Now This campaign is ALL about engaging the good folks in our community.
We want to connect with as many residents in Senate District 14 (ʻĀlewa, Kapālama, Kalihi, Ft.
Shafter, Moanalua, Red Hill) as possible, and we could use your help!
Canvassing is really interesting and easier than you think!
You never knock on doors alone and Christy will always be walking right there with you.
Our goal is to listen to the concerns and ideas of our neighbors and to encourage them to vote in 2026!
If canvassing is not your thing, we would love for you to join us for community sign waving this spring/summer.
It will no doubt be lotsa fun!!
Please sign up to volunteer and see our calendar of events!
Mahalo nui!

added: Reform Oregon’s Death Tax It’s not just the wealthy who pay Oregon’s Death (Estate) Tax anymore.
Claire has worked alongside other Republican leaders in Salem to increase the threshold for this tax to make it less punitive and will continue to do so.
Claire understands that our kids are our future.
She wants to put students first, restore high standards, and ensure Oregon’s education system is focused on student success—not politics or bureaucracy.
Claire’s Plan to Refocus K-12 on Achievement and Empower Parents: Ensure our schools are focusing on the fundamentals of education–reading, writing, and math.
removed: End Oregon’s Death Tax It’s not just the wealthy who pay Oregon’s Death (Estate) Tax anymore.
Claire has worked alongside other Republican leaders in Salem to increase the threshold for this tax to make it less punitive and will continue to push until it is repealed entirely.
And what do Portland and Eugene Democrats choose to prioritize?
Mandating climate change curriculum in our K-12 classrooms.

Claire’s Plan to Refocus K-12 on Achievement and Empower Parents: Ensure our schools are focusing on the fundamentals of education–reading, writing, and math–and repeal burdensome laws like mandated climate change curriculum.

title.after: Education | Clint Collamore

added: top of page Home Blog Events Frequently Asked Questions DONATE Education is Key Education is a complex issue, but vitally important to all of us, even those who no longer have children or grandchildren who are school-age.
Young people are our future.
They are our future doctors, nurses, caretakers, fisherman, farmers, scientists, caretakers, and stewards of this land. ​ I would like to see a renewed belief in the importance of education.
No matter what career path one chooses, fundamental skills in math, science, and language arts are critical.

To run your own business, as many fisherman do, those core skills are essential to success and to the creative thinking that is needed to address the many challenges all of us face in work and our daily lives.
Schools should integrate more in the community.
While Lincoln Academy has a public service requirement for students, Medomak Valley High School does not.
Many of our local groups need volunteers to meet needs, and younger generations need to see the value of this work first hand.

Older students should go to a couple of town Select Board meetings in their community and see how local government works. ​ Perhaps this could be a state-wide initiative to support greater youth involvement as stewards of our beautiful state and how each and every one of us can make differences big and small.
We each play a role in the future success of this state.
For example, people need to understand the impacts of small actions on an our environment.

Citizens need to be reminded that voting is something everyone should do as being part of a community, a state, and a nation. ​ I went to the small elementary school in Bremen, followed by Medomak Valley High School and Region 8 Technical School.
After high school graduation, I followed up with an Associates in business and Bachelor of Science in Public Administration from the University of Maine.
I credit my education not with teaching me everything I need to know in life, but rather laying the foundation for lifelong learning.
I know how to get information, gathering from all sides, and I enjoy continuing to learn and grow as a person.
Education is another space where Federal and State regulations often challenge small local schools and school districts.
This is not to say that all of these laws are bad, but they are often unfunded mandates that can be very demanding on a local school district.

Every single child deserves a free and appropriate education, but some children have enhanced needs and the State and Federal governments should share the burden more fully so that meeting these mandates as the local level doesn't mean losing teachers or educational opportunities for all students. ​ How a Maine State Legislator Can Support Schools ​ A Maine legislator can strengthen public schools by improving funding, supporting student mental health, reducing administrative burdens, investing in workforce development, and ensuring schools have the resources to provide a safe, high‑quality education.
Maine’s education system faces challenges ranging from staffing shortages to rising special‑education costs, and legislators play a central role in addressing them.
Ways Legislators Can Support Maine Schools ​ 1.
Strengthen School Funding & Reduce Local Burdens ​ Maine’s schools rely heavily on local property taxes.
Legislators can help by: Ensuring the state meets or exceeds its 55% school funding obligation.
Increasing support for special education, which is one of the fastest‑growing costs for districts.
Expanding funding for school facilities, including HVAC upgrades, safety improvements, and energy efficiency.
Supporting predictable, stable funding so districts can plan long‑term.
Support Student Mental Health & Well‑Being ​ Maine schools are seeing increased student mental health needs.

A recent legislative proposal ( LD 1123 ) highlighted how many districts struggle to access federal Medicaid funds for school‑based services, with only 45% of districts participating in eligible reimbursements. ​ A legislator can: ​ Fund school‑based mental health professionals, including counselors and social workers.
Improve MaineCare reimbursement support, helping districts access federal funds for services students already receive.
Support partnerships with community mental health providers.
Reduce Administrative Burdens on Schools ​ Schools often struggle with complex state and federal requirements. ​ A legislator can: ​ Streamline reporting requirements.
Fund positions (like the proposed MaineCare coordinators) that help districts navigate complex systems.
Ensure new mandates come with funding (“no unfunded mandates”).

Support Safe, Healthy Learning Environments ​ Legislators can help schools create environments where students can focus and thrive. ​ Examples include: ​ Funding school safety upgrades and emergency preparedness.
Supporting nutrition programs and access to healthy meals.
Supporting programs such as Farm and Sea to School , which benefits students, fisherman, and farmers.
Invest in Teachers & School Staff Maine faces teacher shortages, especially in rural areas. ​ A legislator can: ​ Support competitive salaries and benefits.
Fund professional development and mentorship programs.
Support pathways for ed techs and paraprofessionals to become certified teachers.

added: top of page Home Blog Events Frequently Asked Questions DONATE Frequent Asked Questions This is to address the public's concerns about Clean Elections donations in the past.
General What happened with Clean Elections in 2022/23?
I made a mistake where I accepted $# cash donations from people I know while I was at events such as the Friendship Lobster Boat Races, a yard sale, and didn’t have the forms with me.
The people asked me to just fill it out for them.
I did, with no attempt to disguise my handwriting.
Why were there so many charges?
There were two charges per person who made a $5 donation as there is a list of donations they are supposed to put their name on, as well as an individual slip of paper saying they made the donation.
They dropped the charges on the forged people,because they all did.
Therefore,as a result, it was considered by all as no ill-intent on my part.
What charges did you plead guilty to?
I pled guilty to 12 misdemeanors for filling out the donation slips for real people, who made real donations.
Why did you choose to plead guilty if there was no ill intent?
The court process takes a long time, and is very costly both financially and emotionally.
I wanted it done.
I actually saw a therapist.
I was very embarrassed, and it was hard on my family.
What was your punishment?
From the court, I was given 100 hours of community service.
That was no problem for me as I do that anyway.
I did that at Medomak Exchange and I cleaned veteran’s headstones at Wavus Camps in Jefferson for a weekend.
I also voluntarily paid back all the clean elections money I received, as well as voluntarily paying back money I received for the brief time I was in the legislature.
Why did you resign?
It would take too long to clear my name and I didn’t want it to negatively impact my constituents.
The party made it clear I would have no committees and they didn’t want to work with me.
The Speaker of the House requested that I do.
Why do you think people should trust you now?
It was a mistake and I have learned from it.
The donations were all legitimate and from real people, the mistake was that I filled out the paperwork for the people.
When the State investigated, the 12 people who were contacted all said they had given me the $5, but not filled out the forms.
I also did what I could to make things right.
Many people voted for me knowing the state was investigating because they knew the donations were genuine.
Why are you running again?
Many in the community have asked me to run.
I had no intent to, but as time has gone on, I figured it is now or never.
I want to do it right this time.
People are having issues with rent/housing, heat, food, bills, taxes, just getting by, and the list goes on.
We need people working together to resolve the issues that impact all of us.
There is way too much fighting in Washington, DC, and in Augusta.
This is Maine.
Mainers work together and get things done.
What were the charges against you?
The investigators thought I made up names of individuals who contributed to my campaign.
It was just the opposite.
The contributors all donated and that’s what they found out.
Then I was charged with forging some names even though those contributors requested that I do so.

title.after: Farms | Clint Collamore

added: top of page Home Blog Events Frequently Asked Questions DONATE Family Farms Food is essential to human life, and we all need access to safe, healthy farm products.
Keeping it close to home ensures we retain access.

How a Maine Legislator Can Support Family Farms ​ A legislator has several powerful levers—policy, funding, and regulation—to strengthen family farms, especially around PFAS contamination, drought resiliency, and food sovereignty. ​ 1.
Addressing PFAS Contamination PFAS (“forever chemicals”) have become one of the most significant threats to Maine agriculture.
Contamination has occurred through sludge spreading, groundwater, and other environmental pathways.
Maine has taken national leadership in responding, but the work is ongoing.
Maine’s response includes banning land application of sludge, creating a PFAS Fund , and conducting statewide testing of farms, soils, and water.
Farmers have been directly affected, with some losing herds, crops, or land use due to contamination.
Maine’s agricultural agencies continue to test and support impacted farms.
What a legislator can do: Expand and sustain the PFAS Relief Fund to compensate affected farmers, support income replacement, and fund long‑term monitoring.
Increase funding for soil and water testing, remediation research, and safe disposal of contaminated materials.
Support mental health and financial counseling for affected farm families.
Ensure transparent communication between state agencies and farmers as testing continues.
Strengthening Drought Resiliency ​ Maine has experienced more frequent and severe droughts in recent years, affecting hay yields, livestock feed, irrigation needs, and crop reliability.
Legislative actions that help: Invest in water infrastructure, including grants or low‑interest loans for on‑farm irrigation, ponds, and water‑capture systems.
Support soil‑health initiatives (cover crops, composting, rotational grazing) that improve water retention.
Fund climate‑resilient agriculture programs, including technical assistance through UMaine Extension .
Expand crop insurance access and emergency relief programs for small farms.
Advancing Food Sovereignty Maine is a national leader in food sovereignty , with many towns passing ordinances that give communities more control over local food systems.
Food sovereignty supports family farms by: Strengthening local markets.
Reducing regulatory burdens for small‑scale producers.
Encouraging direct sales and community‑based food systems.
What a legislator can do: Protect and expand Maine’s food sovereignty laws, ensuring small producers can sell directly to consumers without unnecessary barriers.
Support local food infrastructure, such as community kitchens, farmers markets, and small‑scale processing facilities.
Increase institutional purchasing of Maine‑grown food for schools, hospitals, and state facilities.
Promote land access programs for new and beginning farmers.

title.after: Business | Clint Collamore

added: top of page Home Blog Events Frequently Asked Questions DONATE Supporting Local Business Small Businesses are the backbone of the Maine economy.
They make up over 99% of Maine businesses and employ over half of the state’s workforce.
Legislators play a crucial role in strengthening this sector by improving access to capital, reducing regulatory burdens, and supporting workforce and infrastructure development.
While prices are climbing, our small businesses are struggling to make ends meet.
Small businesses are owned by our neighbors and we keep working to help our own economy to grow and be resilient.
Doing this will help younger folks living here and raising their families to be able to find some comfort in living.
Why Small Business is Essential in Maine They make up 99.2% of all Maine businesses.
They employ 290,518 people, representing 54.5% of all Maine employees.
They drive job creation: small businesses contributed 98.5% of net new jobs between 2023–2024.
They support rural communities, local supply chains, and Maine’s identity — especially in tourism, fishing, agriculture, trades, and professional services.
They help stabilize the economy by circulating money locally and fostering entrepreneurship.
Source: U.S.
Small Business Administration Office of Advocacy Why Small Business Matters Even More in Maine Maine’s economy is heavily rural and community-based.
Small businesses keep towns vibrant, provide essential services, and create opportunities where large employers may be scarce.
They also help buffer the state against economic shocks by diversifying local industries.

We need to help our businesses succeed by supporting them, and allowing them easier access to the information that will help them expand and be resilient to changing times. ​ What Legislators Can Do to Support Small Businesses ​ A Maine legislator has several powerful levers to strengthen small business growth and sustainability.
Expand Access to Capital Increase funding for state-backed loan programs and microloans.
Support grants for startups, rural businesses, and innovation sectors.
Encourage partnerships with community banks and credit unions.
Reduce Regulatory Burdens Streamline licensing and permitting processes.
Simplify compliance requirements for very small employers.
Review outdated regulations that disproportionately affect small firms.
Strengthen Workforce Development Invest in vocational training, apprenticeships, and adult education.
Support programs that help small businesses recruit and retain workers.
Expand childcare and transportation access—two major barriers for Maine’s workforce.
Improve Infrastructure Expand broadband access, especially in rural areas.
Support transportation improvements that help businesses reach customers and suppliers.
Promote Local Entrepreneurship Fund small business incubators and technical assistance programs.
Support tourism and local marketing initiatives that highlight Maine-made products.
Encourage youth entrepreneurship and innovation programs.
Support Affordable Healthcare and Benefits Explore incentives for small employers to offer health coverage.
Promote pooled insurance options to reduce costs.

title.after: Fisheries | Clint Collamore

added: top of page Home Blog Events Frequently Asked Questions DONATE Supporting Local Fisheries Fisheries are way over-regulated.
Regulations come from the federal government and by the state.
Every time you turn around they are trying to reduce or close another fishery.
Sometimes these regulations are put forward with no consideration for how they impact heritage industries here in Maine such as lobstering and clamming.
Fishermen have been the conservationist.
They need to be included in all decision-making processes that effect their industry.
We need to stop and reevaluate what is working and what isn't. ​ Until the people that are involved in the industry are at the table, no doubt it will be a failure waiting to happen.
It can't just be legislators and interest groups that aren't directly involved.
As a State Representative, I would be both a legislator and a fisherman fighting for these iconic industries. ​ I was involved in efforts to clean up the Medomak River.
The efforts have shown great success and illustrate how conservation and the fishing industry go hand-in-hand.
The efforts of the Medomak Project helped reopen over 300 acres to clamming, which is a vital economic driver in the district.

This is has not been just a recovery effort, now it is about sustainability. ​ Why Maine's Fisheries Matter Maine’s commercial fisheries—lobster, scallops, groundfish, elvers, aquaculture, and more—are essential because they: Support coastal economies from Kittery to Eastport.
Provide thousands of jobs in harvesting, processing, boat-building, gear supply, and marine trades.
Sustain working waterfronts, which are increasingly threatened by development and climate impacts.
Anchor Maine’s identity, tourism, and food culture.
Contribute significantly to Maine’s export economy, especially lobster.
How a Legislator Can Support Maine Fisheries 1.

Protect Working Waterfronts ​ Working waterfront access is one of the biggest long‑term threats to Maine’s fisheries. ​ A legislator can: ​ Expand the Working Waterfront Access Protection Program to help fishing families and co‑ops secure permanent access.
Support tax incentives or zoning protections for commercial fishing infrastructure.
Fund climate‑resilient upgrades to piers, wharves, and harbors.
Ensure Maine has strong representation in regional fisheries management councils.
Reduce Regulatory Burdens & Improve Communication ​ Fishermen often face complex, rapidly changing regulations.
A legislator can: ​ Advocate for clearer communication between state agencies and fishermen.
Support programs that help small fishing operations navigate licensing, reporting, and compliance.
Ensure that new regulations consider the realities of small‑boat, owner‑operator fleets ​ 3.

Invest in Workforce & Maritime Trades ​ The fishing industry depends on skilled workers—boat-builders, welders, marine engineers, and deckhands. ​ A legislator can: ​ Expand vocational training in marine trades.
Support apprenticeship programs for young fishermen.
Fund safety training, including cold‑water survival and navigation.

added: top of page Home Blog Events Frequently Asked Questions DONATE All Posts Clint Collamore: Bridging Political Gaps in Maine Clinton Collamore Mar 31 4 min read Updated: Apr 2 In a time when political divisions seem to widen daily, Clint Collamore stands out as a beacon of hope in Maine.
His commitment to bridging political gaps and fostering dialogue among diverse groups has made a significant impact on the community.
This blog post explores Collamore's journey, his strategies for uniting people, and the lessons we can learn from his approach.

Understanding the Political Landscape in Maine Maine's political landscape is unique, characterized by a mix of rural and urban populations, progressive and conservative ideologies, and a strong sense of community.
This diversity can lead to misunderstandings and conflicts, but it also presents an opportunity for collaboration and growth.
The Challenge of Division Political polarization is not just a national issue; it affects local communities as well.
In Maine, residents often find themselves at odds over key issues such as healthcare, education, and environmental policies.
This division can create an atmosphere of distrust and animosity, making it difficult for individuals to engage in constructive dialogue.
The Role of Community Leaders Community leaders like Clint Collamore play a crucial role in addressing these challenges.
By fostering open communication and encouraging collaboration, they can help bridge the gaps that divide us.
Collamore's approach emphasizes the importance of listening to different perspectives and finding common ground.
Clint Collamore's Journey Clint Collamore's journey into politics began with a strong work ethic and desire to be an active leader within his community.
He grew up in the town of Bremen, and he still fishes out of there on his lobster boat.

As someone who lobsters and digs clams, he is acutely aware of the balance needed to protect the environment for these heritage industries to thrive, while balancing some of the burdensome regulations that are sometimes brought forward without proper research.
It's a difficult balance, and decisions need to be made with consideration for the fisherman and for long-term sustainability.
Collamore has been active in the successful effort to clean up the Medomak River, which impacts all of the communities in House District 45.
Community Involvement Collamore went to Medomak Valley High School and settled in Waldoboro to raise his children.
In addition to his shellfish conservation activities, he was on the Waldoboro Select Board for 18 years and has served on several other town committees.
Collamore is still a member of the Waldoboro Day Committee where he is in charge of the parade.
He is an avid volunteer who has helped with the Waldoboro Free Clothing Closet and Good Things Thrift & Crafts.
These days people can see him loading cars at the food pantry, and Collamore also helps in less organized ways such as answering the call to help someone finish off a chicken coop.
This past winter he enlisted the help of some friends to put a big lobster trap tree in front of The Waldo Theatre.
It was the first time in over a decade that there was a big tree in the village.
Clint Collamore with Sierra and Buddy Murphy after they constructed a trap tree.
Building Bridges As Collamore's influence grew, he focused on building bridges between different political factions.
He recognized that many residents felt disillusioned with traditional political processes and sought to create an inclusive environment where everyone felt heard.
By inviting individuals from various backgrounds to participate in discussions, he was able to foster a culture of collaboration.
Strategies for Bridging Political Gaps Collamore's success in bridging political gaps can be attributed to several key strategies: 1.
Encouraging Open Dialogue One of the cornerstones of Collamore's approach is encouraging open dialogue.
He believes that honest conversations can lead to understanding and empathy.
By creating safe spaces for discussions, he allows individuals to express their views without fear of judgment.
Fostering Inclusivity Inclusivity is essential in bridging political gaps.
Collamore actively seeks to involve individuals from diverse backgrounds in his initiatives.
This not only enriches the conversation but also ensures that all voices are represented.
We learn a lot from our differences, but only if we listen to each other.
Focusing on Common Goals Collamore emphasizes the importance of identifying common goals.
By shifting the focus from political differences to shared objectives, he helps unite individuals around a common purpose.
This approach fosters collaboration and encourages participants to work together toward solutions.
Most Mainers agree that citizens should all have access to healthcare.
Our environment is important not just for the natural beauty of Maine, but for healthy farms and fisheries that make sure our population is fed.
People want to be able to afford their taxes, to heat their homes, fuel their cars, and make sure their family is safe.
There is so much to build upon.
Utilizing Technology In today's digital age, technology plays a significant role in facilitating communication.
Collamore leverages social media and online platforms to reach a broader audience and engage individuals who may not be able to attend in-person meetings.
This strategy allows for greater participation and inclusivity.
Leading by Example Collamore understands the importance of leading by example.
He consistently demonstrates respect and empathy in his interactions with others, regardless of their political beliefs.
This sets a tone for discussions and encourages others to follow suit.
He admits his mistakes and vows to move forward with new knowledge and continued commitment to his community and to the State of Maine.

added: top of page Home Blog Events Frequently Asked Questions DONATE All Posts Collamore Statement Clinton Collamore Mar 31 2 min read “I intend to run for Maine House District 45 because many constituents asked me to represent them,” Clinton Collamore of Waldoboro said in a statement.
Collamore was elected to the seat in 2022 but resigned after making a mistake with Clean Elections paperwork.
He said he collected some $5 donations from community members and later filled out the paperwork himself not realizing that wasn’t allowed.
“It was an honest mistake for which I have paid dearly.” All the campaign money was paid back, and Collamore says he felt a great deal of embarrassment.

“The hardest part was having my constituents go unrepresented while the issue was sorted out, but they still believe in me and know I care about our communities and our state.” This time, Collamore is running unenrolled.
“Mainers are independent, so it feels like a good fit.” He is also running a traditional campaign this time and has a team on board to help.

“I plan to be present for all votes,” Collamore said, “just as I always try to be present in my community through volunteering and as a former select board member.” Collamore is both a lobsterman and a clam digger, so he is acutely aware of the environmental concerns around Maine’s traditional fisheries.
He also understands the concern for inland waterways and farmlands.
There is a lot of pollution in our waters from old, leaking leach fields and animal waste.
“I will work with the EPA to end the pollution that closes our clam flats and affects the other water critters as well.

“The Maine Emergency Management Agency (MEMA), is surveying drying wells that are causing Mainers to conserve water, have to purchase bottled water, and even drill new or deeper wells,” Collamore said.
“This is a huge and sometimes unmanageable cost for homeowners.” Besides environmental concerns, Collamore said, “I have a few issues that are very important to me.
I want all Mainers to have access to the healthcare they need.
“We also need to make some changes in property taxes so that elderly and fixed income adults are not forced out of their homes because they cannot pay their taxes,” Collamore said.
“It is a tricky issue where there must be income guidelines, and it has to be done in a way that doesn’t shift the burden to younger taxpayers.
This needs to be a state program in order to accomplish that.” “As a father and a grandfather, good education and affordable housing are important to me as well,” Collamore said.
“We need our young people to be able to afford to stay in the communities they grew up in.
Right now, that is hard in each of the towns I would be representing.
“I want to work together with others to find common sense solutions that respect our state’s heritage and keep us moving forward in a positive direction.” Recent Posts See All How to help!

added.text: [image: #Ready to knock some doors and help elect Democrats across Spokane County? Join Carmela Conroy, Callie Gee, Julia Payne, Elliot Robison, and volunteers from across the area for a Spokane Coalition Canvass in Medical Lake this Sunday! Whether you’re an experienced canvasser or have never knocked a door before, we’ll make sure you have what you need to get started. Bring a friend, meet fellow volunteers, and help us reach voters where it matters most—right at their doors. 📅 Sunday, September 20 ⏰ 11:00 a.m.–1:30 p.m. 📍 Medical Lake We need you. Sign up today using the QR code or here: https://www.mobilize.us/conroyforcongress/event/1035813/ and join us Sunday! #Volunteer #Canvass #SpokaneCounty #EasternWashington #wa05 #conroy4congress]

[image: A big shout out to We Have The Power Movement for organizing a Rock the Vote postcard event, and special gratitude to Colleen and Stan Woods for coordinating and making it happen. Our volunteers showed up to help kick off the writing. A room full of people, pens in hand, reminding their neighbors to vote. Thank you, volunteers!]

[image: A few weekends ago, Team Eastern Washington joined Walla Walla Frontier Days Parade, and what a welcome! Neighbors on both sides of the street, kids waving, people stopping us to say what they need from their representative in DC. This is how you earn a district – one conversation at a time. Thank you, Walla Walla!]

[image: A full hall in Usk for the Pend Oreille County Democrats fundraiser – good food, good company, and a couple of dogs who came along for the conversation. Pend Oreille County is big, rural, and easy for Washington, D.C. to overlook. The people here are organized, generous, and paying close attention to this race. Thank you for having me, and for all the work you are doing to turn out every vote up north.]

[image: Are you ready to knock on some doors and help elect great progressive candidates across Spokane County? Join Carmela Conroy, Callie Gee, Rob Tupper, Michaela Kelso, Julia Payne, Elliot Robison, Danny Tarkenton and volunteers from across the area for our Spokane Coalition Canvasses! Whether you’re an experienced canvasser or have never knocked a door before, we’ll make sure you have what you need to get started. Bring a friend, meet fellow volunteers, and help us reach voters where it matters most—right at their doors. We need you. Sign up today at www.conroy4congress.com/volunteer/ #Volunteer #Canvass #SpokaneCounty #EasternWashington #wa05 #conroy4congress]
[image: Canvassing and tabling opportunities are available. If you're in Pend Orielle county, I'll be at the next Pend Orielle county Democrats fundraiser! See you out there! #conroy4congress #wa05]

[image: Days at the Spokane County Interstate Fair, one folding table, an issues spinner wheel, and hundreds of conversations. We talked with lifelong Democrats, lifelong Republicans, and a lot of people who told us they had stopped paying attention. That last group is toughest to reach, but all of our voices matter. Thank you to the Spokane County Democrats and every volunteer who took a shift in that hall. Showing up where people already are beats any ad we could buy.]

[image: Delighted to speak with the Retired Public Employees Council of Washington at their chapter lunch, and to do it at the Longhorn Barbecue. My parents used to take me there before I flew off to overseas assignments, so walking back in felt deeply nostalgic. RPEC members spent their careers serving Washington – in our schools, our hospitals, our cities and our state agencies. They earned their pensions and their health care, and I will defend both in Congress. Retirement security is not a line item. It is a promise. Thank you to RPEC for the invitation, and for the questions – this group does its homework.]

[image: Do you want a Conroy for Congress Yard Sign? Signs can be picked up, during office hours, at our Spokane Campaign HQ, 1106 N. Washington St., Suite B, or the Walla Walla County Democrats office, location and hours at https://www.wallawallademocrats.com Outside of these areas or would like a sign delivered? Contact: volcoord@conroy4congress.com]

[image: Dog day at HQ, and he should have been here. Our volunteers brought their best coworkers, the phones still got dialed, and nobody left without a treat. Come by, bring your (well-socialized) dog, take a clipboard: https://conroy4congress.com/volunteer]

[image: Donald Trump just posted a video attacking me by name as a "dumb-o-crat" and giving Michael Baumgartner his "Complete and Total Endorsement." Trump does not get involved in a race until his party is in trouble. Eastern Washington has his attention because we put this seat in play, and people here are done being taken for granted. But when Trump weighs in, the money follows. This endorsement always brings a surge of cash. I don't have an army of billionaires with an endless supply of dark money. I have you. I spent my career as a prosecutor and a diplomat. I am not intimidated by a man who thinks a social media post decides an election. Help me make sure voters here get the facts instead of Trump's version of them – and we'll win this: https://secure.actblue.com/donate/cc-soc-2609]

[image: Eastern Washington, we’ve got a busy week ahead! 🎉 From Newport to Airway Heights, Lewiston, and Liberty Lake, Carmela will be out meeting voters, canvassing with local candidates, and connecting with supporters across the region. Check out the upcoming events below, grab a friend, and come join us! 💙 We’d love to see you there! Volunteer and donate at www.conroy4congress.com]

[image: Front page of the Seattle Times: "Democrats say U.S. House race is in play." National Democrats consider us a District in Play. Incumbent Michael Baumgartner was the only Republican on the primary ballot, and most voters here voted for change. Nobody handed us this. Volunteers, house party hosts, and neighbors chipping in $26 at a time put this seat on the map. Now let's finish the job. https://secure.actblue.com/donate/cc-soc-2609]

[image: Grateful to the Walla Walla County Democrats for having us at their County Fair booth!. Local volunteers do the unglamorous work – tabling in the heat, signing up volunteers, talking with neighbors nobody has asked for their vote in years. If you are in Walla Walla and want in, we have a place for you: https://conroy4congress.com/volunteer]

[image: Hillyard Pride, and our table was one of the busiest in the park – thanks largely to the volunteers who staffed it and the campaign dog who held down the chair. Eastern Washington is a place where people look after each other. Pride here is neighbors, kids, dogs on leashes, and a community where everyone belongs. I am proud to stand with it, in Hillyard and in Congress.]

[image: Honored to earn the endorsement of the @allianceforgunresponsibility Victory Fund. Every family deserves to feel safe at school, at work, in their place of worship, and in their neighborhood. In Congress, I’ll fight for common-sense gun safety to protect our communities.]

[image: If you haven't voted yet, today is the day! Return your completed ballot to an official drop box by 8pm. Need a replacement ballot in Ferry, Spokane, or Stevens County? Contact your County Elections or Auditor’s Office right away. Stay safe, and let's get out there and vote.‌‌💙]

[image: It's going to be a busy weekend in WA05! Carmela will be at the EWU Neighborfest in Cheney on Friday and there will be canvassing Friday, Saturday and Sunday, in Cheney, Deer Park and Spokane Valley. We need volunteers to staff the Conroy 4 Congress Table at Valley Fest on Saturday and Sunday. To sign up for a shift for two visit www.conroy4congress.com/volunteer/]

[image: James joined his brother Murphy at the campaign office – it's safe to say both are keenly interested in the yard sign situation. Our office runs on volunteers, coffee, and lately a fair amount of dog hair. Come by and say hello. The welcoming committee is ready.]

[image: Join our Election Night Gathering with Team Conroy for Congress! Come gather with our team, connect with fellow supporters, and watch the election results roll in with us at BrickWest Brewing (1318 W. 1st Ave.) from 6:00–9:00 PM.]

[image: Lanterns over the water, neighbors on the lawn, and not one dollar from a corporate PAC. Tonight at midnight the fundraising quarter closes. This is the last report before ballots go in the mail, and it is the number every political reporter and every DC group will use to decide whether Eastern Washington is worth taking seriously. They already decided Trump's endorsement was worth spending on. Let's show them what neighbors chipping in looks like instead: https://secure.actblue.com/donate/cc-soc-2609]

[image: Michael Perry & Eric Horsted opened their beautiful home to us on the Autumn Equinox. String lights, a yard full of neighbors, and – we did not see this coming – aerialists! One of the most memorable nights of the campaign. Everyone who came out that night helped put this race in play. We are so grateful!]

[image: Nearly 300 people participated in person at the #WA05 forum at Whitman College in Walla Walla, and they came with real questions about affordability, health care, and datacenters. Thanks to AAUW Walla Walla and Northwest Public Broadcasting for hosting the forum, and Rasa Vineyards and the Network of Exceptional Women for the after party. We'll be back!]

[image: Now that is craftsmanship. Volunteers across Eastern Washington are building and planting signs on their own land, on their own time, because they want a representative who actually shows up here. Thank you for this one – it is a beauty. Want a sign of your own? https://conroy4congress.com/volunteer]

[image: One of our canvassers knocked on a door in Spokane and left with a loaf of banana bread. This is the part of campaigning that never makes the news. Someone gives up a Saturday, walks a neighborhood, and gets a real conversation and a sweet treat out of it. That is how you win a district Washington, D.C. wrote off. Thank you for the bread, and for the welcome. Want to come with us? https://conroy4congress.com/volunteer]

[image: People took yard signs home all ValleyFest weekend, and every one of them is telling their whole street where they stand. Thanks to everyone who stopped by, the volunteers who kept it running, and especially to Joanne M. Heye for being our photographer! Want a sign of your own? https://conroy4congress.com/volunteer]

[image: Porchfest is Spokane at its best – neighbors on lawns, music on porches, strangers turning into friends by the third song. Thank you to everyone who stopped to talk with us between sets. Being out in community is the best part of being a candidate.]

[image: Rain, shine, and new and returning Eagles. We participated in EWU Neighborfest, walked Cheney in a coalition canvass with Karina Wallace (@karina_justfiguringitout), who is running for State Rep in the 9th LD. Go Team! Students, make your vote count HERE. Register online at VoteWA.gov through October 26, or in person through Election Day.]

[image: Rush hour at Five Mile Plaza, and this is what our campaign looks like: neighbors on a corner, signs in hand, waving at people they have known for thirty years. Nobody paid them. Nobody bused them in. They decided this seat is worth standing on a sidewalk for. If you have ever wanted to help but did not know where to start, this is where to start: https://conroy4congress.com/volunteer]

[image: Spotted downtown: a Silverado with an Air Force plate, a lumber rack, and a Carmela Conroy sign strapped across the back. This campaign does not run on billionaires. It runs on veterans, tradespeople, and neighbors who put our name on their own truck and their own front lawn. Every one of these is somebody publicly announcing their decision. Want one? https://conroy4congress.com/volunteer]

[image: Thank you to everyone who joined Carmela and Team Conroy at BrickWest Brewing on Election Night! With votes still being counted, we're encouraged by the results and energized for the work ahead - join the movement today at conroy4congress.com 💪]

[image: Thank you to our hosts, the Chases and Kuhlings, for inviting your friends to join us! A beautiful old living room, every chair filled, and neighbors who came ready with good questions and stayed long after the last one. Ballots arrive soon! If you would like to host a gathering like this before then, we would love to come: https://conroy4congress.com/volunteer]

[image: Thank you to the Skeims for opening their home to us. A living room full of neighbors, real questions about health care and the cost of living, and no talking points. I would take one of these over a rally any day – you cannot dodge a question in someone's kitchen. If you want to host one before ballots go out, we will bring the buttons: https://conroy4congress.com/volunteer]

[image: Thank you to the Stevens County Democrats for the warm welcome in Chewelah, and to everyone who came out to talk and then headed out to knock doors with us. Rural Eastern Washington is not a flyover on my map – it is the job. Want to canvass with us? https://conroy4congress.com/volunteer]

[image: The Garfield County Democrats set up at the fair with a flip chart and one question: what matters to you this election? Look at what people wrote in. Social Security. Health care. Gas and diesel prices. Food prices. Farming costs. Education. Misinformation. No forever wars. Data centers, and guardrails on AI. Not one person walked up and said culture war. People in Garfield County are worried about the cost of running a household and a farm, and about being told a story instead of the truth. That list is my agenda. Thank you to the Garfield County Democrats for asking the question.]
[image: The writing is on the wall. Literally. #FlipWA05 Let's do this, Eastern Washington.]

[image: There’s a lot happening across Eastern Washington! Carmela is heading to Walla Walla, Spokane, and Spokane Valley, with two upcoming candidate forums and plenty of opportunities to get involved. Check out this week’s events flyer and find a way to join Team Eastern Washington — whether you’re ready to canvass, phone bank, table, or wave signs! Election Day is getting closer. Let’s finish strong!]

[image: VOLUNTEER OPPORTUNITIES!!! If you’ve been thinking about volunteering with Conroy for Congress, now is the time! With Election Day getting closer, there are more ways than ever to help Carmela & local candidates across our community. 🏠 Knock doors with a canvassing team — training is provided, so no experience is necessary. ☎️ Make phone calls from campaign headquarters or from the comfort of home. 👋 Looking for something a little smaller? Wave signs, staff the campaign office, or help at Carmela’s information table at a local event. Whether you have a few hours or want to get involved regularly, there’s a place for you on this campaign. Pick what works for you and sign up today: www.conroy4congress.com/volunteer]

[image: Valleyfest weekend, sharing a booth with "Rational Rob" Tupper, candidate for the 4th LD. We enjoyed lots of good conversations about what people in Spokane Valley need from their representatives. Thanks to everyone who showed up!]

[image: Walla Walla — we need you! Help Carmela Conroy and Derek Sarley and the Vote NO on 645! campaign for two combined canvasses this weekend as we talk with voters and build support across the community. Friday, October 9 | 4–6 PM Sunday, October 11 | 11 AM–1 PM Every door knocked and every conversation matters. Grab a friend, sign up, and come help us finish strong! Sign Up Here! https://www.mobilize.us/conroyforcongress/event/1054338/]

[image: We stopped by Masters Brewhouse in Deer Park on the way home from canvassing in Chewelah, and folks who had seen me at the WA-05 candidate forum waved us over. We talked rising costs, high school sports, and what Eastern Washington needs from its representative in DC.]

[image: Yard signs are flying out the door and new canvassers signing up! Two months from Election Day, this is what it looks like when a district decides it is not sitting this one out. Want a sign, or a door-knocking or phone-banking shift? Sign up at https://conroy4congress.com/volunteer]

If you have ever wanted to help but did not know where to start, this is where to start: https://conroy4congress.com/volunteer

alt://instagram.fhio3-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.82787-15/840589609_17974398468150272_6279657702099450158_n.jpg|Michael Perry & Eric Horsted opened their beautiful home to us on the Autumn Equinox. Everyone who came out that night helped put this race in play. We are so grateful!

alt://instagram.fhio3-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.82787-15/841012494_17974711122150272_5119648225189960708_n.jpg|James joined his brother Murphy at the campaign office – it's safe to say both are keenly interested in the yard sign situation.
