removed: Skip to content Home About Issues News Contact Donate Sign Up Home About Issues News Contact Donate Sign Up Facebook Instagram Congressman Johnson Secures More Than $11 Million For Local Projects Congressman Hank Johnson (GA-04) announced today that more than $11 million in Community Project Funding he secured for Georgia’s 4th District is in the final FY2026 spending bills approved by Congress and signed into law by the president this week.
The funding will directly address some of the most pressing needs across the district, which encompasses most of DeKalb County and parts of Gwinnett County.

Cities within the Fourth District include Stonecrest, Lithonia, Stone Mountain, Clarkston, Tucker, Doraville, Chamblee and Dunwoody in DeKalb County and Peachtree Corners, Norcross, and Duluth in Gwinnett County.
“Taking care of home first has always been my mantra while serving the people of Georgia’s Fourth District,” Rep.
Johnson said.
“The more than $11 million in Community Project Funding will provide a much-needed boost to Georgia’s 4th District.
These investments improve our infrastructure, grow our economy, and improve our greenspace, which makes a real difference in the lives of so many in our community.
I am proud to have fought for funding that will make our community healthier, safer, and stronger.” Rep.
Johnson championed funding for 15 projects that will directly benefit Georgia’s 4th District residents.

These include: $560,000 to DeKalb County for water storage tank fill valve replacements. $1,000,000 to the City of Doraville to make realignment improvements to Chestnut Drive. $850,000 to DeKalb County Parks and Recreation improvements to Wade Walker Park. $1,985,160 to DeKalb County Parks and Recreation for the construction of soccer fields at Avondale Dunaire Park for future tournaments. $1,200,000 to DeKalb County Parks and Recreation for the construction of a new park – Rowland Park – in unincorporated DeKalb with gardens, walking trails and fitness stations. $350,000 to DeKalb County Parks and Recreation for Arabia Mountain bridge improvements. $250,000 to DeKalb County Parks and Recreation for County Line Park Improvements Phase II. $726,625 for DeKalb County government’s Lithonia Booster Pump Station backup power supply to ensure reliable water service during grid disruptions. $850,000 to the City of Tucker for the creation of a multi-use path linking existing trails along Hugh Howell Road with the future South Fork Peachtree Creek Greenway Trail. $250,000 to DeKalb County government for a center for children impacted by domestic violence. $400,000 for MARTA to enhance the safety and security of rail and bus facilities. $1,000,000 for the City of Stone Mountain for improvements to Medlock Park. $560,000 to the City of Brookhaven for Phase II of the Ashford Forest Preserve project. $300,000 to Wellroot Family Services for Reaching Teens Georgia to train local law enforcement, first responders, judges, courts, probation officers, and public defenders in identifying and responding to teens experiencing trauma. $850,000 to Gwinnett County government for the Loop Trail project to improve connectivity between key community destinations, including residential, commercial, recreational, and transit areas.
HERE’S WHAT THEY’RE SAYING “These federal investments will have a meaningful and lasting impact on DeKalb County,” said DeKalb County CEO Lorraine Cochran-Johnson.
“From critical water infrastructure and public safety improvements to expanded parks and recreational spaces, this funding supports quality of life, economic vitality, and community well-being.

We are grateful to Congressman Johnson for his continued advocacy and partnership on behalf of DeKalb residents.” “These investments reflect what’s possible when local priorities and federal partnership align,” said Gwinnett County Chairwoman Nicole Love Hendrickson .
“The Loop Trail project will strengthen connectivity across our communities, making it easier for residents to move between where they live, work, and gather.

I’m grateful to Congressman Johnson for advocating for funding that delivers real, on-the-ground benefits for Gwinnett families.” “MARTA appreciates the continued support and efforts of Congressman Johnson to improve transit infrastructure and enhance safety of the system,” said MARTA Interim General Manager and CEO Jonathan Hunt.

“This funding allows MARTA to implement vital security measures to prevent theft, vandalism, and unauthorized access at our bus and rail facilities, safeguarding customers and employees, and contributing to the long term sustainability of our operations.” “This funding reflects the power of strong partnerships and shared priorities,” said Tucker Mayor Anne Lerner.

“We’re grateful to Mayor Pro Tem Virginia Rece for championing this effort and for Representative Johnson for securing federal support that helps Tucker advance our trail system and strengthens regional connectivity.

Working together across all levels of government allows us to deliver real, lasting improvements for our residents.” “This funding brings to life our vision for Ashford Forest Preserve, which is to ensure this protected Old Growth Forest remains accessible and welcoming to everyone,” Brookhaven Mayor John Park said.
“From ADA parking to accessible restrooms and trails, Phase II represents an important step in opening this preserve to all.

Skip to content Meet Hannah Issues Affordability Education Economic Opportunity Health Care Housing Climate & Energy Accomplishments Endorsements News Volunteer Store Vote Meet Hannah Issues Affordability Education Economic Opportunity Health Care Housing Climate & Energy Accomplishments Endorsements News Volunteer Store Vote Facebook X-twitter Instagram Youtube Tiktok Donate October 12, 2026 Five Questions with Hannah Pingree This column, written by Joyce Vance , was originally published on Substack.
Read it here .
The first time I met Hannah Pingree was at a local parade in Freeport, Maine.
My daughter was working there at the time.
I saw Hannah walking around, casually chatting with folks.
I told her I wasn’t a Maine voter, but I was interested in her ideas for improving housing, which is a real issue for Mainers, as it is for a lot of people across the country.
I was impressed by how substantive her ideas were and the way she talked about them like they were real possibilities—policies she’d pursue if elected, not just talking points.
I’ve paid attention to her ever since.

Hannah, speaking at a recent gathering in Maine Hannah emerged as the winner from a Democratic gubernatorial primary in Maine that was blessed with an abundance of likable, qualified candidates who ran an incredibly collegial race, joking that they’d all work for whoever won at one event.
It was a dose of sanity in the middle of this tense political season, a real respite from the nastiness of Alabama politics.
And a good reminder that people who are in public service for all the right reasons still exist.
We need that right now, especially from America’s governors.
Something we’re seeing is that in the no-guardrails era of would-be king Trump, state leaders have the ability to prevent some of the worst abuses.
Governors have intervened on issues like using the National Guard to police protests and have exerted leadership on a range of issues where national leaders have failed to.
During the final years of Trump’s time in office, it may be governors, along with state attorneys general and secretaries of state, who protect rights like voting and access to medical care.
So I’m especially delighted we have a chance to get to know Hannah better tonight.
We should expect more of our elected officials than the low standards the last decade has left us with.
Talking with Hannah reminds me there is a generation of younger politicians coming along who understand this, and want to deliver.

I love her explanation of what it was like to be the youngest speaker of state in a state legislature anywhere in the country and what she learned from leading the Governor’s Office of the Future in Maine.
“Five Questions” is a Friday feature for paid subscribers, built around the conversations that don’t fit into a news cycle driven by headlines and hot takes.
It’s a chance to spend time with the people shaping the law, politics, and democracy—and to ask the questions that matter most, not just the ones everyone else is asking.
Keeping the daily legal analysis free has always been important to me, and it will stay that way.

These Friday conversations give me a chance to thank paid subscribers for their help ensuring that Civil Discourse remains available to everyone who wants to follow the law beyond the day’s headlines.
Whether you’re a paid subscriber or a free subscriber, I’m grateful you’re here.
Joyce: You’re the youngest woman ever elected to serve as speaker of a state legislature.
Talk with us about that moment, and how it felt to be entrusted with that responsibility?
Hannah: Well, truthfully, I hadn’t planned to run for office at age 25 or to be serving as Majority Leader at age 30 and as Speaker at age 32.
It was an awesome responsibility – and a tremendous honor.
I grew up in a very small island community of just 400 people where you couldn’t wait for someone else to come solve the challenges we faced.
I watched my parents pitch in – on the school board, running businesses, stepping up.
And I saw everyone else in my town doing the same.
It taught me that you have to work with people of all ages, and across the political spectrum, to get things done.
And you can’t give up or wait for someone else to show up.
I also learned that you have to listen and be kind, because even when you have fights or disagreements, the people around you will continue to be your neighbors.
And learning that at a young age gave me a real sense of responsibility, an ability to work with anyone, and a confidence that I could lead other people as well.
So as a very young speaker, I knew I had to be practical, listen, do my homework and work hard, and be willing to collaborate with anyone, Democrat or Republican, who wanted to get something done.
Maine is small enough that you can’t afford to burn bridges.
Like my hometown, you’re going to see those folks at the grocery store or on the sidelines of your kids’ sports games.
I think it’s why I was elected unanimously as Speaker of the House by Democrats, Republicans, and Independents.

I’m proud to have been the youngest woman (sidenote: and the only one in the country to do so while also pregnant) to hold that role, but what I’m proudest of is what we got done together: passed bipartisan budgets, expanded broadband in rural areas, invested in clean energy, lowered health care costs, defended reproductive rights, passed marriage equality, improved housing access, and protected Maine’s working waterfronts.
And even though there were many disagreements, we maintained respect for each other.
Joyce: Under your leadership, Maine became the first state in the country to pass marriage equality.
Barack Obama still wasn’t there, but you were in Maine.
There were legislators who understood the vote might cost them their jobs but still thought it was important to do the right thing.
Can you talk about what gave you all the courage to move ahead in that moment and whether leadership like that still exists?

Hannah: I think about that moment a lot, and I often say that helping lead the fight for marriage equality taught me one of the most important lessons I’ve learned in politics: you have to be brave, especially when the decisions you’re making matter so deeply to people’s lives and families.
When I got married back in 2007 to my husband, two dear friends of mine, David and David, helped marry me.
But, they couldn’t legally get married themselves.
They could celebrate my marriage, but they weren’t entitled to the same rights and protections for their own relationship.
That was personal to me, and it was fundamentally unfair.
And here’s what makes that story especially poignant today.

David and David finally got married just this past year, not because they suddenly decided their relationship mattered more, but because they were worried about what Donald Trump and his administration might do to their rights.
After all these years, they still felt they needed to protect their family from the possibility of losing rights we fought so hard to secure.
Back in 2009, we knew passing marriage equality would be politically difficult.
There were legislators, including Democrats, who were nervous about taking that vote.
Some knew it might cost them their seats.
But they did it anyway.
I’m enormously proud of those colleagues, because they understood that there are moments when doing what’s right matters more than protecting your political future.
That experience shaped me as a leader.
It taught me that courage isn’t about being fearless.
It’s about knowing something matters enough that you’re willing to take a risk for it.
And when you’re talking about people’s families, their dignity, and their fundamental rights, that’s exactly what elected leaders should be willing to do.
Does that kind of leadership still exist?
Absolutely.
I see people in the Maine leadership and communities making difficult decisions and standing up for their neighbors – especially over the course of the last few years.
Whether it is standing up for immigrant neighbors who are being terrorized by ICE or taking politically difficult votes in the Maine legislature.
I also think this moment demands more courage from all of us.
We are watching rights that generations of Americans fought for come under threat, and we can’t afford to let political calculations determine whether we stand up for the people who need us.
I’ve always believed you can be principled and pragmatic at the same time.
You can fight hard for what you believe in and still work with people who disagree with you.
That’s how I approached my work in the Legislature, and it’s how I would approach being governor.
Joyce: You’ve also served on your local school board, a role many people think is one of the most important in government.

How did you get there, and what do you think about the role of local government in making people’s lives better, and how important you think it is to elect committed people to school boards nationwide?
Hannah: I often joke that serving as chair of my local school board was the hardest job I’ve had in politics, but it’s true!
I was elected as I was leaving the Legislature and having my first child, and I went on to serve nine years.
Now, with two teenagers in Maine public schools, I’ve experienced public education as a student, a parent, and a board chair.
And I’ve never seen the challenges facing our schools and school leaders feel more urgent.
I think school boards are one of the most important places where public service happens, because you’re entrusted with something incredibly precious: other people’s children and their futures.
And you’re making decisions that affect your neighbors every single day.
It’s an enormous responsibility.

You’re trying to make sure every child gets a great education, that students who need extra support aren’t left behind, and that teachers and school staff, who are often your friends and neighbors, are treated fairly and paid a wage that allows them to live in the communities they serve.
At the same time, you’re accountable to taxpayers, including seniors and working families who are struggling to afford their property taxes.
Those are real tensions, and there aren’t always easy answers.
And in the last few years, school boards have faced an entirely new set of challenges.

We’ve seen national political fights brought into local classrooms, debates over books and curriculum, attacks on LGBTQ students and educators, and growing pressure on people who are simply trying to do right by their communities.

All while schools are dealing with the very real challenges of student mental health, learning loss, staffing shortages, and preparing kids for a future being transformed by technology and artificial intelligence.
I worry that some of the loudest political battles distract us from what should be our shared responsibility: making sure every child feels safe, supported, and challenged to reach their potential.
You can disagree about education policy, and people certainly do, but we should never lose sight of the kids at the center of those decisions.
That’s also what I love about local government.
It’s personal.
In a small Maine town, the people making decisions are your neighbors.
You see them at the grocery store, at school events, and around town.
You have to listen, explain your decisions, and live with the consequences alongside everyone else.
So yes, I think it’s incredibly important that good people step up to serve on school boards, especially now.

We need people who care deeply about public education, who respect teachers and parents, who are willing to listen to different perspectives, and who won’t let national political divisions get in the way of doing what’s best for children.

Serving on my school board reinforced something I’ve believed throughout my career: government works best when people show up, take responsibility, and care enough about their neighbors to do the hard work.
That’s true in a small-town school board meeting, and it’s just as true in the governor’s office.
Joyce: You’ve told the story of outgoing Maine Governor Janet being so taken with the Kurt Vonnegut quote that “every government ought to have a Department of the Future” that she created one.
And you got to play a role in it.
Explain that to us; tell us what you were involved with and how this shapes your view of the role of government.
Hannah: I was the first director of the Governor’s Office of Policy Innovation and the Future or GOPIF.
Governor Mills was inspired by that Kurt Vonnegut quote and the previous governor had eliminated the state’s Planning Office, so we were essentially building something new from scratch.
But it truly was an office focused on the future and how we ensure thoughtful planning as well as collaboration, to get to policy solutions for some of the most critical issues facing Maine.
One of the things I’m proudest of is the incredible team we built.
We hired smart, creative, deeply committed people who wanted to tackle some of Maine’s toughest challenges.

And we approached the work with a pretty simple philosophy: bring people together who don’t always agree, listen to the people closest to the problems, use good data and evidence to guide decisions, and be transparent about what we’re trying to accomplish and whether it’s working.
We took on some of the biggest challenges facing Maine, from housing and workforce shortages to climate change, economic development, and the needs of children and older Mainers.
None of these problems could be solved by one agency or one political party.

We brought together local leaders, businesses and workers, advocates, scientists, and people with very different perspectives to develop new approaches and turn them into real policies and investments.
And we delivered results.

We helped make Maine a national leader in heat pump adoption, advanced climate and storm resilience efforts, developed new approaches to housing and workforce challenges, and helped communities and businesses navigate the pandemic and economic recovery.
We weren’t afraid to try innovative ideas, measure what was working, and change course when something wasn’t getting results.
But maybe the biggest lesson I took from that experience is that you can’t give up on the hardest problems.
Housing, climate change, the opioid crisis, the challenges facing working families—these aren’t things you solve with one bill, one budget, or one press conference.
They require sustained attention, honest conversations, collaboration across agencies and political lines, and a willingness to keep pushing even when progress is frustratingly slow.
And it’s how I would lead as governor.
I don’t think Maine people expect the government to solve every problem overnight.
But they have every right to expect us to be creative, accountable, and relentless about making things better.
Leaders shouldn’t just respond to the next crisis.
It should be building the future we want for our kids and our communities.

Joyce: From talking with Mainers, it seems to me that one of the secrets to the high regard you’re held in is that in an era where people tend to think of government as broken, you expect it to be functional and you get things done.
I’ve heard you say that ability makes you hopeful about Maine’s future.
Are you hopeful about the country’s future too?
Hannah: Well, that’s very kind.
I’d say I’ve been lucky to work with a lot of good people who also wanted to get things done.
And yes, I’m hopeful.
I’ll admit it’s not always easy right now.
I think Donald Trump has done enormous damage to our country, to our institutions, and to the basic sense of decency and respect that should guide how we treat one another.

But I also think his presidency has reminded millions of Americans just how precious some of our most fundamental values are: democracy, freedom, the rule of law, and the belief that everyone deserves dignity and opportunity.
These aren’t things we can take for granted, and I see people standing up to defend them every day.
I’ve always believed you can’t lead if you’re not hopeful.
How can you take on the hardest problems and ask people to join you if you don’t believe things can get better?
But hope has to be matched with action.

When you roll up your sleeves and actually solve something, whether it’s a school budget, a housing project, or helping a community recover from a storm, it gives you another reason to believe in what’s possible.
And I see that spirit in Maine all the time.
People show up for each other.
They coach the team, run the community supper, serve on the school board, and help neighbors through tough times, regardless of their politics.
That’s the country I believe in, and I don’t think Donald Trump gets to define who we are as Americans.
So yes, I’m hopeful.
Not because I think things will magically get better, but because I believe there are still far more people who want to build something better than tear it apart.
And I’ve seen what can happen when we bring those people together and get to work.
“People show up for each other.” Isn’t that what this great American experiment is all about?
There is some simple, elegant wisdom in Hannah’s words, and I appreciate that final point she makes, that Donald Trump does not get to define who we are as Americans.
We do.
We’re in this together, Joyce Spread The Word Let's Go!

Democrat Hannah Pingree is the heavy favorite in the Maine governor’s race, a New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll found — the first public survey to be conducted since the June primaries.
Pingree, a former speaker of the Maine House of Representatives and an official in Gov.
Janet Mills’ administration, has the support of 50% of likely voters, according to the poll.
Republican Bobby Charles received 36% support, followed by independent Rick Bennett, who received 8%.
The poll, which surveyed 608 likely voters between June 19-26, gives a preview of how the race to November could go and the impact that Bennett’s third-party candidacy will have.
It had a margin of error of +/- 4.8%.
A former Republican who unenrolled from the party when he got in the race a year ago , Bennett has been seen as most likely to draw moderate Republican voters from Charles, a MAGA-style candidate .
According to the polling, most of Bennett’s support comes from voters who identify as independents.
Among those who identified as Democrats, 3% said they were likely to vote for Bennett, compared to 6% of Republicans and 12% of voters who identified as independents.
Pingree performed the best with independent voters.
She pulled 47% of those who identify as independents, while Charles got 31%.
Nine percent said they were not sure whom they would support for governor or didn’t answer the question.

When voters were asked to pick between just Pingree and Charles, or volunteer a different candidate they planned to support, Pingree’s lead over Charles increased, suggesting that Bennett is pulling slightly more from Pingree’s supporters than Charles’.
Fifty-five percent of respondents picked Pingree over Charles in the one-on-one matchup, with Charles drawing 40% support.
Four percent said they didn’t know who they would vote for or didn’t answer the question, while less than 1% volunteered a different name.

Dennis Reeves, a retired pastor from Sanford and an independent voter who participated in the poll, said he is likely to support Pingree “not because I necessarily agree with her on many things, but because I won’t support anyone who supports Trump.” Pingree has made pushing back on President Donald Trump a key issue in her campaign, while Charles has sought to align himself with the president.
Bennett voted for Trump in 2016 , but has not supported him more recently.
He hasn’t made the president a big talking point on the campaign trail.
Reeves, a former Republican who said he changed his registration after Trump was nominated for the presidency in 2016, said he didn’t know much about Bennett.

He noted that he doesn’t agree with Pingree’s support for allowing transgender athletes to compete in girls’ sports — an issue that conservatives are trying to bring to a statewide referendum in November.
Bennett, a state senator from Oxford, voted last year against bills aimed at preventing transgender athletes from competing in girls’ sports.
Charles has expressed support for the referendum seeking to ban trans athletes from participating on teams that don’t match their gender at birth.
“Obviously I’m going to have to vote for somebody I don’t totally agree with,” said Reeves, 78.

“I’m going to make my decision based on character and their willingness to follow the law and follow the Constitution.” Kirsten McQuillan, a real estate broker from Sidney and a registered Democrat, is backing Pingree — though she said she has also voted for Republicans in the past, including U.S.
Sen.
Susan Collins in 2020.
She said she looks for “the right person and the person who has a good moral compass” in elections.
In the governor’s race, she wants someone who will address key issues such as affordable housing and who will take a humanitarian approach to the job.
“I like her presence,” McQuillan, 50, said of Pingree.
“She has a good commanding presence and is trustworthy.

In this crazy political environment, we need someone who has their head on straight and has commonsense values.” In Aroostook County, Charles supporter Daniel Deveau said high energy costs are a key issue for him, and he feels the Republican candidate will take the right approach to bring them down.
Charles’ energy plans include reforming Maine’s Public Utilities Commission and negotiating completion of key natural gas pipelines.
Deveau, a retiree from Cyr Plantation, is optimistic about Charles’ chances.
He thinks the candidate’s message will resonate particularly in rural Maine, but said it could be a tough race.
“Now you have an independent in there, so who knows what’s going to happen,” he said.
Independents make up about one-third of Maine voters, and the state has a history of supporting them for key offices.
One of four members of Maine’s congressional delegation, U.S.
Sen.
Angus King, is an independent.
King also served as an independent governor from 1995 to 2003.
All of Maine’s recent gubernatorial elections dating to 2010 have featured independent candidates, though how much support they’ve received has varied widely.
In the last election for governor, in November 2022 , retired doctor and political outsider Sam Hunkler received about 2% of the vote in a race featuring incumbent Gov.
Janet Mills and former Gov.
Paul LePage.
In 2010, independent Eliot Cutler, a lawyer and lobbyist, finished second to LePage in a five-way race in which he received close to 36% of the vote.
LePage won with 38%.
The New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll of Maine voters was funded with support from the Maine Trust for Local News.

In the survey released Thursday, Pingree wins in a photo finish with Shah with 52% of votes to his 48% after a ranked-choice simulation.
But more than 1 in 10 voters were still undecided in the first round, showing a deeply uncertain race given the ranked-choice voting dynamics.
Pingree and Jackson are in a ranked-choice voting alliance that is vying to overcome Shah.
Shah and Jackson have gone toe-to-toe with both campaigns alleging “shady” tactics in recent days tied to dark-money PAC ads and messaging about each other’s records.
A pair of recent polls have shown Jackson surging late in the election.
This is the first poll showing Pingree separating from Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, who is in the alliance with Pingree and Jackson but was in fifth place with just 11% first-choice support.
Former clean energy executive Angus King III was the top choice for 14% of Democrats.
Bellows notched the fewest first-choice votes and dropped first in the poll’s ranked-choice simulation.
When undecided voters are set aside, her votes are reallocated and King drops, the contest narrows further, with Shah at 36% of the vote, Pingree 33% and Jackson 31%.
While a plurality of Jackson voters tap Bellows as their second choice, they prefer Pingree as their third choice over Shah, giving her the overall narrow lead in the final round of the simulation.
However, small shifts in the electorate could swing the race.
For example, her voters look poised to break for Shah rather than Jackson if she is the third candidate eliminated.

Senate candidate Graham Platner could hold some power in the final days of the campaign.

Rep.

Pingree, who is endorsed by Mills , was the top choice of 27% of the early voters who have already cast a ballot, which was 12% of respondents, SurveyUSA said.

When I turned 30, suddenly all of my friends were talking about buying houses.
Or, more specifically, how hard it is to buy a house.
Looking at houses on Zillow in one’s spare time is no longer a fun game; it’s just depressing.
So many house prices have skyrocketed since 2020.
Due to Maine’s housing prices, I see myself sticking to renting for a good long while.
That’s not to say, of course, that renting is necessarily easier.
Rents in Portland rival those in Boston.
And outside of Portland, we don’t find much relief either.
But at least when my dishwasher breaks, I’ll have someone to call.
Hard to save for that down payment, though.
Thankfully, we have someone running for governor who knows Maine is facing a very serious housing crisis.
Hannah Pingree’s housing plan will invest in housing, stop out-of-state corporations from driving up rents and cut the red tape that slows development.
Hannah’s smart, clear and comprehensive housing plan gives me hope for Maine’s future.

Charlie Dingman is the chair of the Maine Democratic Party and an attorney based in Augusta.
He lives in Leeds It will surprise no one that, as chair of the Maine Democratic Party, I enthusiastically support our Democratic nominee for governor, Hannah Pingree.
But my support for Hannah goes well beyond my role as party chair.
It comes from watching her work for years and seeing firsthand the kind of leader she is.
I have spent much of my career as a lawyer advocating before all three branches of Maine government.
That has given me a front-row seat to state government, both when it works well and when it doesn’t.
It has given me the opportunity to see Hannah’s effective leadership during her time in the Legislature and her work leading the Governor’s Office of Policy Innovation and the Future.
Hannah listens, asks insightful questions, and thinks strategically.
She works with focus, determination, and courage to build workable solutions.
And I believe she will stand up to anyone who, like our current president, would stand in the way just to accumulate wealth and power.
Good leadership is not just about having the loudest voice in the room.
It is about understanding the problems we face, listening to people affected by them, and figuring out how to make things better.
That has been a consistent focus of Hannah’s career.
My career has long focused on health care law and policy, so I find Hannah’s approach to that key public concern especially encouraging.
Our health care system is enormously complex, often chaotic, and insufficiently focused on health outcomes and affordability.

Maine people feel the chaos, cost, and inadequacy as they struggle to afford insurance, find a primary or specialty care provider, or maintain prescription drug therapy when it’s prohibitively expensive.
Ideal solutions will require concerted, nationwide action and investment.
Hannah knows we can’t wait for Washington to get there, which may take years even after we reawaken Congress by sending Democratic majorities to the House and Senate.
That’s why she’s pledging to create a public health insurance option in Maine.

It will not eliminate private or employer-sponsored coverage but will provide another choice — a state-backed plan designed to provide affordable, reliable coverage and use the state’s leverage to help bring down costs.
Her health care plan recognizes something that is especially important in Maine: having coverage does not mean much if you cannot find someone to care for you.
She has proposed investing in primary care, strengthening maternity and reproductive health care, and recruiting and retaining more health care workers, particularly in rural communities.
I believe Hannah is the leader we need to seek real improvements in this challenging arena: a governor willing to dig into the details and stay focused on getting results.
We can’t ignore the extraordinary headwinds that any state leader will face from what I view as our currently corrupt and self-absorbed federal government.

President Donald Trump’s Republicans have concentrated wealth and power by funding their tax cuts for the ultra-rich with massive cuts to health care and other basic services, while brutally attacking rights and institutions we have long taken for granted.

I think Maine needs a governor who will resist these abuses of power, acting creatively to counteract them to the full extent that a state can do so, while we await a reckoning and a change in direction in Washington.
I believe Hannah has the tenacity, the energy, the intelligence, and the compassion we need to lead Maine in this incredibly challenging chapter of our history.
The next four years will bring challenges we can predict and, undoubtedly, some we cannot.
Maine needs a governor who cares deeply about the people they serve and knows how to turn good ideas into action.
I’ve seen Hannah Pingree deliver exactly that for years in her other leadership roles.
I’m excited to be working to elect her as Maine’s next governor.

removed: top of page 53RD DISTRICT REPRESENTATIVE • TOPEKA, KS VOTER REGISTRATION OFFICIAL LEGISLATIVE PAGE KIRK HASKINS STATE REPRESENTATIVE Home About Kirk Priorities Get Involved In the News DONATE WHO IS KIRK HASKINS Rooted in Topeka , fighting for Kansas.
From a family of educators, veterans, and community volunteers to the Kansas Statehouse, Kirk Haskins has never stopped serving the people of Topeka.
Learn more about the background and values that drive him every day.
FAMILY BACKGROUND AND TOPEKA ROOTS ​Kirk is a native Topekan who grew up in the Kenmore neighborhood and has resided in the 53rd District for more than 20 years.
Kirk’s father, Forrest, is a Korean War Marine Veteran who grew up in a farm family outside Lindsborg, and he is a retired USD 501 educator who proudly served as the Topeka - NEA President.
Kirk’s mother, Pat, is a retired state employee who grew up in a farm family in Vermillion, KS.
Forrest and Pat are inducted into the Kansas State Square Dance Hall of Fame and spent many hours, over many years, dancing and volunteering in service to that community.

KIRK'S EDUCATION Kirk attended Potwin Elementary, Robinson Middle School, and graduated from Topeka High, where he was on the football team as a tight end and linebacker, and participated in Debate and Forensics.

He was a member of Topeka High’s 1989 Forensics State Championship Team, and he credits retired Topeka High educator Pam McComas for encouraging and inspiring his public speaking skills. ​ Kirk holds a B.A. in Communications with minors in Business and Theatre from Washburn University, an M.B.A. from Wichita State University, and an Ed.D. in Higher Education Administration from the University of Kansas.
KIRK'S PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE Kirk’s professional life began in movie theatre management at West Ridge Mall 6.
He continued this work in Wichita while pursuing his M.B.A., but during his time in Wichita he transitioned to working for Youth Entrepreneurs of Kansas, ultimately becoming their Program Director.

This position was the first to bring together the two primary themes of Kirk’s professional experience — business and education — as he wrote curriculum for, and mentored high school student business entrepreneurs.
Kirk returned to Topeka to work at his alma mater, Washburn University, as the Director of Student Affairs for the School of Business.

After a few years, he transitioned to the University’s Director of Admissions for seven years, before moving on to be the Business Education Consultant for the Kansas State Department of Education (KSDE).

In this role, Kirk wrote the Kansas high school business education curriculum and traveled the state supporting our business educators in developing instructional objectives that met both federal and state business education curriculum standards.

After five years at KSDE, Kirk was recruited to the private sector as the Senior Vice President for Retail Operations at CoreFirst Bank and Trust, where he made positive impacts on employee retention and cash error reduction with changes to onboarding training and thorough mentoring.
After almost two years there, Kirk turned his focus to completing his doctoral dissertation, and while doing so, worked for USD 501 as a building substitute for Jardine Elementary.
Soon after graduating with the Ed.D. from KU in 2018, Kirk became Associate Professor and Chair of Professional Graduate Studies for Baker University, the position he currently holds.
In addition to teaching, he is engaged in program and curriculum development, as well as supporting students and faculty colleagues.
Kirk was a very proud Uncle when conferring a degree to his niece at the May 2024 Baker graduation!

Court Pauses Kansas Law Eliminating Three-Day Mail Ballot Grace Period Kirk Haskins Jul 16 2 min read A Kansas court delivered a significant win for voters this July, temporarily blocking the Republican-backed law that eliminated the three-day grace period for mail-in ballots — a law Kirk has been fighting against since it was first introduced.
A judge in the District Court of Douglas County granted a temporary injunction on July 16, halting Senate Bill 4 from applying to upcoming elections.
The injunction requires election officials to allow a three-day grace period for advance mail-in ballots postmarked on or before Election Day.
The lawsuit was brought by Kansas Appleseed Center for Law and Justice, Loud Light, and the Disability Rights Center of Kansas.
The groups argued the bill disenfranchised older adults and Kansans with disabilities, making it very difficult to vote by mail.
KSNT The stakes are real.
If the 2025 law had been in place in November 2024, more than 2,100 ballots that arrived at county offices in Kansas during the three-day period would have been disqualified.
The grace period was originally enacted in 2017 on a 40-0 vote in the Senate and a 123-1 vote in the House, and was signed into law by a Republican governor.
Republicans later reversed course, passing SB 4 to eliminate it.
Gov.
Laura Kelly vetoed the bill, but the House voted 84-41 and the Senate voted 30-10 to override her veto.

Attorney General Kris Kobach announced his intention to file an emergency appeal to the Kansas Supreme Court, calling the injunction "unprecedented" and "poorly-reasoned." The Supreme Court ultimately declined to take the emergency appeal, leaving the injunction in place ahead of the August 4 primary.
Kirk has consistently opposed SB 4 and the broader pattern of voting restrictions coming out of the Kansas Statehouse.
This ruling is a reminder that the fight to protect your right to vote is far from over.

Haskins Pushes Back on Constitutional Amendment Over Non-Citizen Voting Kirk Haskins Jun 19 1 min read Rep.

Kirk Haskins voiced strong opposition to a proposed constitutional amendment that would add language to the Kansas Constitution specifying that only U.S. citizens are eligible to vote — a protection that federal law already guarantees.
Kansas lawmakers passed HCR 5004, a proposed constitutional amendment that will appear on the November 3 general election ballot.
A yes vote would amend the Kansas Constitution to state that only a U.S. citizen is eligible to vote in the state.
KSN Kirk argued the amendment is unnecessary and potentially harmful.
Haskins referenced testimony from the Secretary of State's general counsel about a 2018 federal court case that found claims of voter fraud in Kansas were bogus.
That case revealed five instances in a 20-year period in which someone who wasn't a U.S. citizen possibly had voted in Kansas, out of millions of votes cast.
Kirk also raised concerns about the chilling effect the amendment could have on naturalized citizens.
"If I was a non-citizen and I've successfully become a citizen, but yet you keep scrutinizing over whether I can vote, I'd likely just say that I don't want to take the risk.
I'm not going to go," Haskins said.
"They should feel open and free to vote and express their voice." Haskins and other Democrats complained that the amendment appears to be an attempt to drive GOP turnout in the election cycle.
"Folks, we got other issues we need to focus on," Haskins said.

"If you want to devote attention to this issue to drum up turnout for elections, let's talk about how we can make voting more available." removed: top of page 53RD DISTRICT REPRESENTATIVE • TOPEKA, KS VOTER REGISTRATION OFFICIAL LEGISLATIVE PAGE KIRK HASKINS STATE REPRESENTATIVE Home About Kirk Priorities Get Involved In the News DONATE WHERE KIRK STANDS Prioritizing Kansans every single day.
At the Statehouse, Kirk Haskins has stood up for voting access, public schools, and fair policies that put people over politics.
As Ranking Minority Member on the House Elections Committee, he’s led the fight against voter suppression and worked to ensure every Kansan’s voice is heard.
AFFORDABILITY Making Kansas More Affordable Kansas should be a place where working families can keep more of their hard-earned money and easily build a future.

Kirk is fighting to lower living costs for Kansas families by cutting taxes on everyday essentials, reducing utility and healthcare expenses, and delivering direct property tax relief for homeowners and renters.
VOTING RIGHTS Securing Your Right to Vote Every eligible Kansan deserves a voice — and Kirk has spent his time in Topeka making sure that voice isn't silenced.

As Ranking Member of the House Elections Committee, he has been on the front lines opposing every bill designed to make it harder for Kansans to cast their ballot, register to vote, or have their vote counted.

EDUCATION Protecting Our Public Schools ​ Strong schools don't happen by accident — they happen when legislators show up, fight for funding, and refuse to let public education become a political punching bag.
Kirk has done exactly that.

From fully funding K-12 classrooms and fighting for teacher due process rights, to supporting the behavioral health resources that students increasingly need just to get through the school day, Kirk believes that investing in Kansas kids is the single best investment the state can make.
HEALTHCARE Healthcare That Works for Every Kansan Too many Kansans are one diagnosis away from financial disaster.
Kirk believes access to quality, affordable healthcare is not a privilege reserved for those with the right job or the right zip code — it is something every Kansas family deserves.

From expanding Medicaid to reforming the prior authorization process that delays care for patients who need it now, Kirk has been a consistent voice for putting patients ahead of insurance company profits. press to zoom press to zoom press to zoom press to zoom 1/1 "By investing in our local communities, we support our families and ensure a strong, sustainable future for Kansas." - REPRESENTATIVE KIRK HASKINS Kirk Haskins REPRESENTATIVE - 53RD DISTRICT 1430 SW Woodhull St., Unit 3911 Topeka, KS 66604 ​ haskinsforkansas@gmail.com (785) 289-8530 Home | About Kirk | Priorities | Endorsements Updates Get Involved | Press Kit Privacy Policy | Terms | Accessibility STAY INFORMED Receive legislative updates and campaign news from Kirk directly.

added: 0 Skip to Content About Terry Issues Donate Open Menu Close Menu About Terry Issues Donate Open Menu Close Menu About Terry Issues Donate Text Message Privacy Policy This privacy policy has been compiled to better serve those who are concerned with how their ‘Personally identifiable information’ (PII) is being used online.

PII, as used in US privacy law and information security, is information that can be used on its own or with other information to identify, contact, or locate a single person, or to identify an individual in context.
Please read our privacy policy carefully to get a clear understanding of how we collect, use, protect or otherwise handle your Personally Identifiable Information in accordance with our website.
What personal information do we collect from the people that visit our blog, website or app?
When ordering or registering on our site, as appropriate, you may be asked to enter your name, email address, mailing address, phone number or other details to help you with your experience.
When do we collect information?
We collect information from you when you register on our site, place an order, subscribe to a newsletter, respond to a survey, fill out a form or enter information on our site.
How do we use your information?

We may use the information we collect from you when you register, make a purchase, sign up for our newsletter, respond to a survey or marketing communication, surf the website, or use certain other site features in the following ways: To improve our website in order to better serve you.
To allow us to better service you in responding to your customer service requests.
To administer a contest, promotion, survey or other site feature.
To quickly process your transactions.
To send periodic emails regarding your order or other products and services.
To show promotions and offers via social media platforms like Facebook and Instagram.
How do we protect visitors’ information?
We use vulnerability scanning and/or scanning to PCI standards.
We use Malware Scanning.
We use an SSL certificate Do we use ‘cookies’?
Yes.

Cookies are small files that a site or its service provider transfers to your computer’s hard drive through your Web browser (if you allow) that enable the site’s or service provider’s systems to recognize your browser and capture and remember certain information.
For instance, we use cookies to help us remember items in your shopping cart and process your order.
They are also used to help us understand your preferences based on your previous or current site activity, enabling us to provide you with improved services.
We also use cookies to help us compile aggregate data about site traffic and site interaction so that we can offer better site experiences and tools in the future.
We may also use trusted third party services that track this information on our behalf.
You can choose to have your computer warn you each time a cookie is being sent, or you can choose to turn off all cookies.
You do this through your browser (like Internet Explorer) settings.
Each browser is a little different, so look at your browser’s Help menu to learn the correct way to modify your cookies.
Third Party Disclosure We do not sell, trade, share, or otherwise transfer to outside parties your personally identifiable information unless we provide you with advance notice.

This does not include website hosting partners and other parties who assist us in operating our website, conducting our business, or servicing you, so long as those parties agree to keep this information confidential.
We may also release your information when we believe release is appropriate to comply with the law, enforce our site policies, or protect ours or others’ rights, property, or safety.
However, non-personally identifiable visitor information may be provided to other parties for marketing, advertising, or other uses.
California Residents California Online Privacy Protection Act CalOPPA is the first state law in the nation to require commercial websites and online services to post a privacy policy.

The law’s reach stretches well beyond California to require a person or company in the United States (and conceivably the world) that operates websites collecting personally identifiable information from California consumers to post a conspicuous privacy policy on its website stating exactly the information being collected and those individuals with whom it is being shared, and to comply with this policy. – See more at: http://consumercal.org/california-online-privacy-protection-act-caloppa/#sthash.0FdRbT51.dpuf According to CalOPPA we agree to the following: Users can visit our site anonymously Once this privacy policy is created, we will add a link to it on our home page, or as a minimum on the first significant page after entering our website.
Our Privacy Policy link includes the word ‘Privacy’, and can be easily be found on the page specified above.

Users will be notified of any privacy policy changes: On our Privacy Policy Page Users are able to change their personal information: By emailing us By calling us By logging in to their account How does our site handle do not track signals?
We honor do not track signals and do not track, plant cookies, or use advertising when a Do Not Track (DNT) browser mechanism is in place.

COPPA (Children Online Privacy Protection Act) When it comes to the collection of personal information from children under 13, the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) puts parents in control.

The Federal Trade Commission, the nation’s consumer protection agency, enforces the COPPA Rule, which spells out what operators of websites and online services must do to protect children’s privacy and safety online.
We do not specifically market to children under 13.

Fair Information Practices The Fair Information Practices Principles form the backbone of privacy law in the United States and the concepts they include have played a significant role in the development of data protection laws around the globe.
Understanding the Fair Information Practice Principles and how they should be implemented is critical to comply with the various privacy laws that protect personal information.

In order to be in line with Fair Information Practices we will take the following responsive action, should a data breach occur: We will notify the users via email Within 1 business day We will notify the users via in site notification Within 1 business day We also agree to the individual redress principle, which requires that individuals have a right to pursue legally enforceable rights against data collectors and processors who fail to adhere to the law.

This principle requires not only that individuals have enforceable rights against data users, but also that individuals have recourse to courts or a government agency to investigate and/or prosecute non-compliance by data processors.

CAN SPAM Act The CAN-SPAM Act is a law that sets the rules for commercial email, establishes requirements for commercial messages, gives recipients the right to have emails stopped from being sent to them, and spells out tough penalties for violations.

We collect your email address in order to: • Send information, respond to inquiries, and/or other requests or questions. • We may also send you additional information related to your product and/or service. • Market to our mailing list or continue to send emails to our clients after the original transaction has occurred.

To be accordance with CAN SPAM we agree to the following: • NOT use false, or misleading subjects or email addresses • Identify the message as an advertisement in some reasonable way • Include the physical address of our business or site headquarters • Monitor third party email marketing services for compliance, if one is used. • Honor opt-out/unsubscribe requests quickly • Allow users to unsubscribe by using the link at the bottom of each email PAID FOR BY TERRY HATTON FOR STATE REPRESENTATIVE © # Hatton for State Representative.

added: Charlotte Wilcox Mayor, Highland Village ENDORSEMENT 08 As Mayor of Northlake, I appreciate Representative Richard Hayes' willingness to engage directly with local mayors and take the time to understand the challenges our communities face.
With the tremendous growth occuring across Denton County, decisions made in Austin have a real impact on our towns and residents.
Richard recognizes the importance of listening to those of us working through these challenges at the local level.
His accessibility, open communication, and genuine interest in understanding our concerns are qualities I value in a state representative.
Brian Montini Mayor, Town of Northlake ENDORSEMENT 09 I have known Richard for many years and have had the opportunity to serve alongside him on numerous board and for community organizations.

Carl Anderson President, North Texas Fair and Rodeo Association ENDORSEMENT 09 If there is a Veteran candidate running for office, should a Veteran voter cast their vote for the Veteran, just because?
Please note, the best candidate should receive your vote.
As a Veteran and voter my vote for best candidate will be made for Richard Hayes.
Serving Denton County means showing up, listening, and delivering results.
From property tax, relief and economic development to investments in roads and water infrastructure, Richard has worked to address the issues that matter most to our communities.
His commitment to everyone in Denton County remains strong.
Whether a Veteran or civilian of the community, Richard Hayes is a proven leader.
Reelect Richard Hayes for Texas House district 57.
Paul Bastaich USAF, Retired ENDORSEMENT 09 The American Icon, Abolitionist, and Republican Leader, Frederick Douglass stated about the necessity of critical leadership.
“We have to do with the past only as we can make it useful to the present and the future." Richard Hayes, epitomizes this statement.

His dedication, leadership skills, work ethic and ability to get constructive and forward leaning bills passed into law; empowering the Great State of Texas to lead when others are either to afraid or to insecure to act.
As such, Chaplain Rich Stoglin, fully endorse Richard Hayes, for reelection to District 57 as State Representative for the Great State of Texas!

Donate Voting Information Register to Vote Qualifications to Register to Vote be a United States citizen; be 18 years old by December 31 of the year in which you file this form (note: you must be 18 years old by the date of the general, primary or other election in which you want to vote); live at your present address at least # days before an election; not be in prison or on parole for a felony conviction and; not be adjudged mentally incompetent by a court; not claim the right to vote elsewhere. ​ How and Where to register to Vote ( Deadlines ) You can register in person at your county board of elections or at any New York State Agency-Based voter registration center.
You can enter your name directly into our mailing list database to have a New York State Voter Registration Form mailed to you.
(NOTE: The same form can be downloaded, using the link below.) You can call our 1-800-FOR-VOTE hotline to request a voter application.
You can download a PDF version of the New York State Voter Registration Form.
Download English Form ( 279KB) Download Spanish Form ( 300KB) Print the form, complete and sign it, and mail it to your county board of elections .
Alternately, you can complete a PDF version of the New York State Voter Registration Form on-line by clicking on the link below, typing the necessary information and selecting the appropriate boxes.
However, the file size of these forms are substantially larger than the above forms, so it may take quite a while for them to load on computers with slower Internet connections.
Complete English Form On-line ( 426KB) Complete Spanish Form On-LIne ( 330KB) Once the form is completed, you need to print the form and sign it.
We cannot accept any kind of digital or Adobe-generated signature.

Then, mail the form to your county board of elections . ​ Absentee Voting Qualifications to Vote by Absentee Ballot Absent from your county or, if a resident of New York City absent from said city, on Election Day.
Unable to appear at the polls due to temporary or permanent illness or disability; or because you are the primary care giver of one or more individuals who are ill or physically disabled.
A patient or inmate in a Veterans' Administration Hospital.
Detained in jail awaiting Grand Jury action or confined in prison after conviction for an offense other than a felony.
How to Vote by Absentee Ballot ( Deadlines ) Applications for Absentee Ballots are available at your county board of elections.

You may also download a PDF version of the New York State Absentee Ballot Application Form Download English Form ( 261KB) Download Spanish Form ( 145KB) Upon completion, applications must be mailed to your county board no later than the seventh day before the election or delivered in person no later than the day before the election.
You may also request an Absentee Ballot by sending a letter to your county board of elections.
The letter must be received by your county board no earlier than # days and no later than seven days before the election.

The letter must contain the following information: the address where you are registered an address where the ballot is to be sent the reason for the request, and the signature of the voter An application form will be mailed with your ballot.
The application form must be completed and returned with your ballot.
If you cannot pick up your ballot, or will not be able to receive it through the mail, you have the right to designate someone to pick it up for you.
Only that person designated on your application may pick up and deliver your ballot.
If you are permanently ill or disabled, you have the right to receive an Absentee Ballot for each subsequent election without further application.
Simply file an application with your county board of elections indicating permanent illness or physical disability.
You will then automatically receive an absentee ballot for every election until your registration is canceled.

Military and Overseas (Federal) Voting Military Voting Qualifications Persons serving in the military, along with their spouses and/or dependents, may register as a military voter in New York, entitling them to receive an absentee ballot for all federal, state and local races that they would be otherwise entitled to vote in if they were to go to their assigned polling place based on their New York residence.

Registering/Applying for a Ballot To register as a new military voter and/or to request an absentee ballot, you must complete a Federal Post Card Application and return it to your county board of elections in New York.
This application will register you (if not already registered) and will also serve as your absentee ballot application for 2 federal general election cycles.
Always be sure to share any change of address information with your county board of elections .

Applications are available from your Voting Assistance Officer on base, or you can visit either the Federal Voting Assistance Program Website or the Military and Overseas Federal Voting Website for forms and information.
On this application, you may state a preference as to how you would like to receive your ballot.
You can choose mail, fax or email as a preferred method of transmission.

If you have stated a preference to receive your voting materials by email/online, you will receive an email notification directing you to the State’s online ballot delivery site, https://ny.secureballotusa.com to access your ballot.
Questions?

Call the State Board of Elections at 518-473-5086 or the Federal Voter Assistance Program at 1-800-438-8683, or contact your Voting Assistance Officer or US Embassy office. *All information listed above is taken directly from the NYS Board of Elections website, found here .

Log In Donate About Our Movement Our Mission Meet EL-MAHDI Georgia State Representative El-Mahdi Holly was elected into public office in 2018, by building a broad coalition of local support to earn his seat by a solid majority vote - making history as both the 1st person of color and the 1st Democrat to win his historically Republican semi-rural district. ​ Known locally as “EL”, Representative Holly has proudly called Henry County home since 2003.

Raised in Georgia by his father, a Christian minister and businessman, and his mother, a local college professor, Holly was taught the importance of active voluntarism in serving the community and solving problems at a very early age.
After being awarded the National Youth Service Award from President Bill Clinton for his efforts mentoring young teens, Holly pursued and received a Bachelor of Arts from Morehouse College .
He went on to earn a Masters of Public Administration from University of West Georgia .

A proud member of Tabernacle of Praise Church in McDonough, Holly has maintained an active daily schedule, attending to the needs of his local constituents, including city & county officials, while also engaging members of Georgia’s business community to help provide better life opportunities . ​ Since being elected in 2018, Representative Holly has sponsored & co-sponsored 206 pieces of legislation , founded the Georgia Africa Legislative Caucus (the 1st in the nation) to support minority business growth, passed a law outlawing and penalizing worker misclassification, granted multiple authorities for his counties, and has won numerous recognitions including the coveted “ Legislator of the Year ” awards from The Georgia Council on Developmental Disabilities (2022) and The Georgia Legislative Black Caucus (2023-2024).
He is also the proud sponsor of the Annual BLACK MEN & BOYS DAY , in partnership with Black Male Initiative Georgia and The Black Man Lab at the State Capitol.
PROUDLY ENDORSED BY Improving the outcomes for working families demands real time and effort.
El- Mahdi cou ld not have gotten this far without the support of believers like you .

View Event → Jun 29 BACK TO THE MAJORITY: Virtual Fundraiser with Lea Thompson Monday, June 29, 2026 7:00 PM 8:00 PM Google Calendar ICS Great Scott - we’re going Back to the Majority!
I am beyond thrilled to share that Lea Thompson, Rochester’s own, Lorraine McFly herself, is joining us rural DFL House candidates to help flip seats and restore the DFL majority .

Join Back to the Future star and southern Minnesotan Lea Thompson for a virtual fundraiser on: 📅 Monday, June 29 🕖 7:00 PM 🎟️ Tickets begin at just $25, and sponsorship opportunities are available at $88, $250, $500, and $1,000+ levels.
To join the host committee, please contact: [email protected] A Zoom link will be sent to the email address associated with your contribution on the day of the event.
One of the unique things about this event is that contributions can be split among participating candidates or directed to the candidate(s) of your choice.
Simply select the "customize amounts" option when making your contribution.
RSVP and Donate Together, we're working to rebuild support for Democrats in rural Minnesota, strengthen our communities, and create a future where every town has a voice at the Capitol.

View Event → Jun 27 Community Events Rochesterfest Parade Saturday, June 27, 2026 12:00 PM 2:30 PM Google Calendar ICS Join Team Heather and the DFLs of Olmsted County to walk in the Rochesterfest Parade! 📅 Saturday, June 27th 🕒 Lineup at 12:00 PM 📍NW side of Soldiers Field Park 🤝 With DFLs of Olmsted County RSVP Here .

removed: top of page Steve Holm - FOR MN HOUSE - Home About Get Involved Contact Holm for House - Bring It Holm - Home is where we raise our families, tend our land, and look out for our neighbors.
It's where we expect clean water, honest work, and a doctor when we need one.
For too long, the issues that matter most to District 20B have taken a back seat to noise from Washington.
It's time to bring the focus back where it belongs — home.
GET INVOLVED Become Part of Our Movement DONATE LEARN MORE VOLUNTEER - Bring It Holm - Steve Holm for Minnesota House District 20B I grew up on a small farm outside St.
Charles.
I learned early that when something breaks, you don't wait around for someone else to fix it — you figure it out yourself, with whatever you've got.
That's the mindset I carried through 41 years at Mayo Clinic, seven years on the Saratoga Township Board, and every volunteer hour I've put into this community.
And it's the mindset I'll carry to St.
Paul. ​ District 20B is my home.
You are my neighbors, my friends, my co-workers.
I've worked beside you, waved at you on the highway, and sat across the table from you at township meetings.
I've seen your hard work and your resilience.

I've also seen your struggles — the farm families piecing together second and third incomes just to stay afloat, the folks driving long distances for basic medical care, the quiet worry about what we're leaving behind for the next generation. ​ You deserve a representative who understands those struggles because they've lived them too.
Someone who will take your concerns seriously, fight for practical solutions, and never lose sight of the people back home. ​ That's what this campaign is about.
Not party politics.
Not talking points.
Just a neighbor asking for the chance to serve — and a promise to bring it home.

removed: top of page Steve Holm - FOR MN HOUSE - Home About Get Involved Contact ABOUT STEVE Already Your Neighbor Steve Holm isn't a career politician, and he'll be the first to tell you so.
He's a farm kid from St.

Charles who grew up learning that hard work, resourcefulness, and looking out for your neighbors aren't just good values — they're survival skills. ​ Steve was born and raised in rural Minnesota, and though life took him in many directions, District 20B has always been home.
He's the kind of person who never really left, because this community is woven into who he is.
Problem-Solver By Nature Growing up on a farm, Steve learned that there's almost always a solution — even if you have to get creative to find it.

That instinct followed him into a 41-year career at Mayo Clinic, where he started as a computer operator and worked his way up to Lead Analyst Programmer, managing teams enhancing the Electronic Medical Record system.

Along the way, he identified an operational change that saved Mayo thousands of dollars, helped double the size of the Help Desk team through a training program he co-developed, and led projects that improved both healthcare efficiency and patient safety.
He worked alongside physicians, nurses, and staff at every level — because he understood that the best solutions come from listening to the people closest to the problem.
A Public Servant At Heart Steve's commitment to community runs deep and long.
He served on the original Saratoga Township Planning and Zoning Variance Board, then spent seven years as an elected Saratoga Township Supervisor.
He currently serves on the Winona County Planning and Zoning Board, sits on the MiEnergy Advisory Committee, and serves as president of two local cemetery associations.
When the American Rescue Plan Act became available to townships during COVID, many Minnesota townships walked away from the daunting paperwork.
Steve didn't.
He navigated the IRS filing requirements and secured over $62,000 for Saratoga Township — funds that went toward a bridge replacement, upgraded parking lot access, and new road gravel.
That's Steve in a nutshell: he does the work, even when it's hard, because he knows his community is counting on him.
Why He's Running ​Steve was approached by community leaders and asked to represent the DFL in District 20B.
After talking it over with his family and reflecting on a lifetime of local service, the answer was clear.
This was the next logical step — a chance to serve his state with the same dedication he's given his community for decades.
He's not running to make a name for himself.
He's running because 20B deserves a voice in St.
Paul — and he believes that voice should belong to someone who cares deeply about the future of this place we call home.
MISSION STATEMENT Bring It Holm Home means something to people in District 20B.
It's the land your family has worked for generations.
It's the neighbor who shows up when things get hard.
It's the small town where everybody waves, everybody helps, and everybody knows that what happens here matters — even if St.

Paul doesn't always act like it. ​ For too long, the issues closest to our daily lives have been drowned out by political noise from Washington and overlooked by legislators who don't know what it's like to watch a farm family struggle, drive forty-five minutes to a clinic, or worry about what's getting into the groundwater.
That stops now.

I'm Steve Holm, and I'm running for Minnesota House District 20B because I believe the people of this district deserve a voice that sounds like theirs — plain-spoken, solutions-focused, and grounded in real experience.
Whether it's protecting our water, making farming viable again, growing our regional economy, or ensuring every rural resident has access to healthcare, these are not abstract policy debates to me.
These are the realities of the community I grew up in, worked in, and have served for decades. ​ Minnesotans are responsible, resilient, and above all, good neighbors.
We have always had what it takes to solve our own problems.
It's time to stop waiting for someone else to fix things and bring the focus back where it belongs — home.

Snohomish County, Ballots are in the mail.
Vote early and drop your ballots off at your local drop boxes.
I'm honored to share that Congressman Rick Larsen has endorsed my campaign for the 39th District.
Rick is the top Democrat on the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, and he knows how much roads, bridges, transit, and freight matter to families in Snohomish and Skagit ... counties.
Getting to work, getting kids to school, and getting goods to market all depend on infrastructure that's safe and well funded, from the Highway 2 trestle to Highway 20 and every route in between.
Rural communities too often get left out of those conversations.
Fixing that takes good relationships at every level: federal, state, county, and city.
No one level can do it alone, and the projects that get built are the ones where everyone is at the table.
That kind of collaboration is what I've done my whole career, and it's what I'll bring to Olympia.
Thank you, Congressman Larsen, for your trust and support.
Thank you to first responders, schools, union sisters and brothers, Veterans, farmers, small business owners, and the community as a whole!
It's been such a pleasure talking with everyone at the doors.

I've ... appreciated the broad range of support from Democrats, Independents, and some Republicans who value the skills, experience, and relationships I will bring to Olympia to stay solution focused and bring people together for our communities.

Here is the Skagit County Auditor's website for ballot information: https://www.skagitcountywa.gov/government/auditor-s-office/elections-and-voting/ballot-information/ #WA39 #IdaforWa #GOTV 2 0 Share 1108195102383524_122117678618631455 Follow Ida Keeley for WA #ago Lightbox link for post with description Earlier this week, I had the opportunity to ...
Earlier this week, I had the opportunity to attend Leadership Day hosted by Leadership Snohomish County at the beautiful Tulalip Tribes Resorts ballrooms.
Leadership Snohomish County runs leadership development programs for emerging and established leaders across sectors.
It's non-partisan ... and attracts leaders from business, nonprofit, and government to grow and hone their leadership skills.
Participants build skills in areas like purpose, decision-making, and equity, and join a network of 1,000+ alumni committed to servant leadership and community impact.
There were great speakers, plenty of chances to network, and it was wonderful seeing so many friends and making new ones.

Congratulations to the award winners: Community Award: Washington West African Center, led by Executive DirectorPa Ousman Joof, for their leadership in helping feed, educate, and nurture the community, and for always showing up whenever and for whatever is needed.
Deborah Knutson Woman in Leadership Award: Rosario Reyes, for all her outstanding accomplishments with the Latino Education Training Institute (LETI).

Distinguished Alumni Award: Ryan Crowther, for his mentorship of others and his leadership as founder of the Everett Music Initiative, which brings Everett together through Music at the Marina and the Fisherman's Village Music Festival.
Every person in our district is stronger when leaders show up for each other and for the people around them, and these honorees do exactly that.
Thank you Adrianne Wagner, Elena Cervantes, and Kathy Solberg for the outstanding work you do growing leaders in our State!

But I want to say clearly where I stand.
I've spent my career in child welfare, juvenile justice, courts, government budgeting, and nonprofits, and I know how these systems connect (or don't).
When we cut ... community supports, the cost doesn't disappear.
It shifts to ERs, first responders, and the housing and homelessness crisis.
Families lose stability, and kids lose the consistency, routines, and medications they depend on.
When children and family systems lose that support, they are no longer low risk.
They can escalate into higher cost systems like foster care, intensive residential services, and institutional care.
We have a culture where we are trained to respond to crisis instead of investing in prevention, and prevention costs less than crisis response.
In the end, taxpayers, hospitals, first responders, social workers, and behavioral health providers pay the price of these cuts.
2,655 neighbors is not a line item.
I'll be fighting for them in Olympia.

added: alt://idaforwa.com/wp-content/plugins/social-wall/img/placeholder.png|Earlier this week, I had the opportunity to attend Leadership Day hosted by Leadership Snohomish County at the beautiful Tulalip Tribes Resorts ballrooms. Leadership Snohomish County runs leadership development programs for emerging and established leaders across sectors. It's non-partisan and attracts leaders from business, nonprofit, and government to grow and hone their leadership skills. Participants build skills in areas like purpose, decision-making, and equity, and join a network of 1,000+ alumni committed to servant leadership and community impact. There were great speakers, plenty of chances to network, and it was wonderful seeing so many friends and making new ones. Congratulations to the award winners: Community Award: Washington West African Center, led by Executive DirectorPa Ousman Joof, for their leadership in helping feed, educate, and nurture the community, and for always showing up whenever and for whatever is needed. Deborah Knutson Woman in Leadership Award: Rosario Reyes, for all her outstanding accomplishments with the Latino Education Training Institute (LETI). Distinguished Alumni Award: Ryan Crowther, for his mentorship of others and his leadership as founder of the Everett Music Initiative, which brings Everett together through Music at the Marina and the Fisherman's Village Music Festival. Community matters. Every person in our district is stronger when leaders show up for each other and for the people around them, and these honorees do exactly that. Thank you Adrianne Wagner, Elena Cervantes, and Kathy Solberg for the outstanding work you do growing leaders in our State! #WA39 #IdaForWA #community #LSC

alt://idaforwa.com/wp-content/plugins/social-wall/img/placeholder.png|I'm honored to share that Congressman Rick Larsen has endorsed my campaign for the 39th District. Rick is the top Democrat on the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, and he knows how much roads, bridges, transit, and freight matter to families in Snohomish and Skagit counties. Getting to work, getting kids to school, and getting goods to market all depend on infrastructure that's safe and well funded, from the Highway 2 trestle to Highway 20 and every route in between. Rural communities too often get left out of those conversations. Fixing that takes good relationships at every level: federal, state, county, and city. No one level can do it alone, and the projects that get built are the ones where everyone is at the table. That kind of collaboration is what I've done my whole career, and it's what I'll bring to Olympia. Thank you, Congressman Larsen, for your trust and support. #WA39 #IdaforWA #Transportation #trestle #hwy2 #hwy20

But I want to say clearly where I stand.
I've spent my career in child welfare, juvenile justice, courts, government budgeting, and nonprofits, and I know how these systems connect (or don't).
When we cut ... community supports, the cost doesn't disappear.
It shifts to ERs, first responders, and the housing and homelessness crisis.
Families lose stability, and kids lose the consistency, routines, and medications they depend on.
When children and family systems lose that support, they are no longer low risk.
They can escalate into higher cost systems like foster care, intensive residential services, and institutional care.
We have a culture where we are trained to respond to crisis instead of investing in prevention, and prevention costs less than crisis response.
In the end, taxpayers, hospitals, first responders, social workers, and behavioral health providers pay the price of these cuts.
2,655 neighbors is not a line item.
I'll be fighting for them in Olympia.
