One of the most important lessons I've learned over the past 24 years, since our son Reece was diagnosed with severe autism, is that disability can touch any family at any time.
We are all just one unexpected moment away from needing the same supports and services that so many rely on today.
Until disability affects you or someone you love, it's often difficult to fully understand how complex, challenging, and overwhelming navigating these systems can be.
That's why it's so important that we continue to listen, learn, and advocate for policies and services that help every member of our community live with dignity, opportunity, and support.
21 Jul Tuesday, 12:01 PM · 2026 Brad attends Rochester Area Chamber of Commerce's Linking Leaders & Industry event at Chick-fil-A Miracle Mile.
It was an honor and a privilege, as a candidate for Minnesota House District 25A, to attend the Rochester Area Chamber of Commerce's Linking Leaders & Industry event at Chick-fil-A Miracle Mile.

I want to extend my sincere thanks to Matt and Crystal Stockdale, Owner/Operating Partners, for sharing both their personal journey to becoming Chick-fil-A franchisees and the inspiring story behind the Chick-fil-A brand.
Their presentation highlighted the company's strong values, commitment to servant leadership, and dedication to making a positive impact in our community.
Chick-fil-A employs more than 200 team members across its two Rochester locations, with an annual payroll of approximately $3 million.

Beyond serving great food, they are deeply invested in our community through partnerships with Community Food Response, Channel One Regional Food Bank, and by providing more than 200 meals each month to pediatric patients at Mayo Clinic.
Matt and Crystal also shared valuable insights into the economic challenges facing local businesses with candidates seeking local, county, and state offices.
I appreciated the opportunity to hear firsthand how government policies affect employers and the business community.

Among the topics discussed were: • Rochester's EV charger requirement, which requires one EV charging station for every 50 parking spaces, even when demand is limited. • Extending the allowable work hours for 14- and 15-year-olds from 7:00 p.m. to 9:00 p.m., which they described as a significant opportunity to better support their workforce. • The financial impact of implementing Minnesota's Paid Family and Medical Leave program. • The need for a more streamlined and accessible pathway to citizenship for individuals who want to live and work in our communities. • Housing affordability and the rising cost of living, which continue to affect employees and employers alike.
These are important conversations that deserve thoughtful discussion at every level of government.
Working together, we can identify practical solutions that help businesses grow, support employees, and strengthen our local economy.
Thank you again to Matt and Crystal, the entire Chick-fil-A team, and everyone who made this event possible.
Your commitment to your employees, your customers, and the Rochester community is truly inspiring.
Thank you for welcoming us into your story, sharing your experiences as franchise owners, and demonstrating what it means to lead with integrity and service.
Thank you, Rochester Area Chamber of Commerce, for creating this opportunity for us candidates.
It was “my pleasure” to learn more about the Chick-fil-A organization and to express my appreciation for everything Chick-fil-A does to make Rochester a stronger and more caring community.

15 Jun Monday, 3:27 PM · 2026 Vehicle Registraton Costs; Wisconsin vs.
Minnesota This is unacceptable for Minnesotans.
The current formula-based system needs to be re-evaluated.
On top of the base registration tax, drivers are also paying a stack of additional costs, including plate fees, filing fees, technology surcharges, and public safety fees.

While funding roads and bridges is essential, and vehicle registration revenue is directed into the Highway User Tax Distribution Fund (HUTDF), the current structure places an uneven burden on Minnesota drivers.
There was some work done on this this year, but it doesn't take effect until January 2027, with some fees reverting back to 2023.
More work needs to be done, however.

If elected to represent MN House District 25A, I will work across the aisle to reform this system and pursue a more reasonable, transparent flat-fee model, similar to what most other states use for vehicle registration.

added: I've been a registered nurse since 2012.
I spent years as a travel ICU nurse, and when COVID hit, I felt called to serve on the front lines.
I was there when families said goodbye over phones held up at the bedside.
At the bedside I watched people skip medications, put off a diagnosis, and go into debt over a single ER visit.
You don't forget that, and it's a big part of why I'm running.
I live paycheck to paycheck in a one-bedroom with my dog and two kittens.
I'm not a career politician, and I don't have a Super PAC.
This campaign is people-funded, so the only people I'll owe are you.
Here at home I founded the CAMP Rehoboth Cares Committee and served as Secretary of the Eastern Sussex Democrats.
I learned that politics works best neighbor to neighbor.
My values are simple.
Every person has dignity.
We should live with moral wholeness, so that what we say matches what we do.
And we have to see the world as it is and as it could be at the same time.
I can't close my eyes to the hard parts, and I won't give up on the better version.
Right now too much of our system is built to keep people out.
Exclusionary systems lock in fees, paperwork and red tape.
Crony capitalism lets the people with money write the rules for everyone else.
I want an economy that works for the people doing the work.
That's why I'm fighting for: Justice and accountability.
I want full, independent investigations, with the facts and the courts deciding.
An end to forever wars.
Congress, not the president, decides when we go to war.
Every dollar spent on endless war is a dollar taken from Delaware families.
Student debt forgiveness for all, and free education going forward, with fully funded public schools.
Stop trapping people in old debt, and stop manufacturing new debt.
Health care and housing for everyone, with the richest Americans and the biggest corporations paying their fair share.
Real rules for AI.
That means independent safety testing before release, liability when products cause harm, protections for workers, and data centers paying their own power bills.
A safe, clean environment.
I stand with Beyond Pesticides.
In the Senate I'll cosponsor the pesticide warning-label bill and the Opportunities in Organic Act.
I'll fight for polluter-pays PFAS cleanup and a PFAS ban under the international definition.
The companies that poisoned our water should pay to clean it.

My training: a BSN from Frostburg State University; associate degrees in Arts and in Science from Hagerstown Community College; and Occupational Studies in Massage Therapy from the Heritage Institute.
Read the full platform → Write me in on November 3 Find the U.S.
If there's an oval or box next to it, fill that in too.
removed: I live paycheck to paycheck in a one-bedroom apartment with my dog, Aurora, and my kittens, Leo and Luna.
I recorded my campaign introduction video on my lunch break, and that's still how this campaign runs: on a phone, with no Super PAC and no party machine.
Where I come from I was born in Hagerstown, Maryland, and grew up on a farmhouse porch just over the line in Welsh Run, Pennsylvania.
I'm the middle of three boys in a working-class family.
My parents met in the Navy.
My dad spent twenty years as a correctional officer at the Hagerstown prison, and my mom was a freight dispatcher.
At seven I got a piano for Christmas and found out I could play by ear.
When I was eight, a bad case of mono led to lesions on my brain.
During a biopsy at the University of Maryland, I had a stroke.
I spent weeks in a coma and woke up unable to speak, then spent months relearning to walk and talk.
It took about three years to get my speech back, but I didn't quit.
A nurse who cared for me in that hospital is the reason I became a nurse.
I wanted to pay it forward.
I came out when I was thirteen.
I paid for it.
I was kicked out of more than one school, and opportunities were taken from me.
I kept going anyway.
As a teenager I bused tables at a crab house in Halfway, Maryland, to help my mom with the bills.
I learned early that an institution can decide you're inconvenient, and that you can outlast it.
Years at the bedside Massage therapy was my first career out of high school, meant to pay for medical school, until the Great Recession took that work away.
So I became a nurse.
I worked my way up the ladder the long way: floor nursing first, then step-down, then critical care.
At Meritus Medical Center in Hagerstown, a patient's family nominated me for the DAISY Award for extraordinary nurses, and I won.
"Travis has a wonderful bedside manner and is very professional.

He stood out among many of the nurses we have come across over the years." "He definitely is a role model… He was a blessing through our experience." — A patient's family, DAISY Award nomination, Meritus Medical Center I spent years as a travel ICU nurse, four years in all.
My first year was in ICUs at several hospitals in Las Vegas.
Then I spent three years in the ICU at David Grant Medical Center on Travis Air Force Base in California, a Department of Defense hospital.
I cared for service members and their families, people who had put themselves on the line for this country.
Serving them was an honor.
In 2019 the base commander awarded me a commander's coin for reporting a mistake I had made, even though speaking up put me at risk.
Owning my errors is how I was trained to keep patients safe, and it's the same accountability I'll demand in the Senate, starting with my own.
After that, a travel assignment brought me to Delaware, as a recovery-room (PACU) nurse at Beebe Hospital.
I'd loved Delaware since childhood vacations, and I made my home here.
When the pandemic hit, I kept my Delaware home and felt the call to go to the front lines and serve my country, working in a COVID unit at Cooper University Hospital in Camden, New Jersey.
Nurses held up phones so families could say goodbye to patients they weren't allowed to visit.
Cooper University Hospital, Camden, 2020.
Before a shift, 2020.
COVID broke something in me, and I left the bedside.
Leaving felt like failing.
It wasn't.
Good nurses around me left too, because the system asked more than people can give.
At the bedside, I watched people skip medications, put off a diagnosis, and go into debt over one ER visit.
That's a big part of why I'm running.

What colleagues say "His clinical knowledge and skill set him apart early… He oriented six of our new staff, both civilian and active duty military." — Critical Care Flight Commander, David Grant Medical Center (USAF) "He has never wavered in his dedication to each of his patients and their families." — Nurse, 60th Surgical Operations Squadron, David Grant Medical Center (USAF) "He is the employee that any manager would love to have on their staff." — Regional Chronic Care Coordinator, Roxbury Correctional Institution Starting over This wasn't my first time rebuilding.
The recession took my first career, and the pandemic nearly ended my second.
So I went back to massage therapy here in Rehoboth, and that's my work now.
I know you can build again.
Leo and Luna, supervising from my lap.
My neighbors I live near Rehoboth Beach, where I put myself back together.
I sing baritone with CAMP Rehoboth Chorus, and I still play piano.
I've volunteered with local nonprofits and helped organize a rally in Rehoboth Beach for International Women's Day, and I kept showing up.
I help guide Benevolent Community Initiative circles with my mentor Lori Ann — neighbors building communities worthy of our shared humanity.
Singing a solo with CAMP Rehoboth Chorus.
Why I'm running This campaign started in a room where I wasn't allowed to ask a question.
Senator Chris Coons was speaking.

I wanted to ask him about the Iran war and the billions in military aid to Israel he voted for in 2024, and about the money his campaign has raised from AIPAC's PAC and its donors, and from defense-contractor PACs.
I was told I couldn't.
The message was that we have to be nice to those in power.
I don't believe that.
Standing up to people in power, politely and without fear, is the whole point of a democracy.
If a constituent can't ask a senator a hard question, somebody needs to ask it from the ballot.
So I decided to challenge him myself.
Getting your name printed on the ballot for U.S.
Senate here costs a $10,000 filing fee.
For someone living paycheck to paycheck, that's out of reach.
I didn't think anyone should have to pay it for the right to run.
So I filed as a declared write-in.
The Delaware Department of Elections lists me as a Qualified write-in candidate for U.S.
Senator, which means your write-in vote for me is counted and reported.
Since then I've written more than a hundred daily letters to Delaware.
At the U.S.
Capitol, 2024.
What I'll fight for 1 Justice and accountability.
I want full, independent investigations into possible crimes and self-enrichment in this administration.
Then the facts and the courts decide.
2 Ending the wars.
Congress, not the president, decides when this country goes to war.
3 Regulating AI.
AI is being rolled out with almost no rules.

David Robinson, who led the writing of OpenAI's safety reports, wrote on October 3: "If this is the situation, then the time for trial and error is over." I'll fight for independent safety testing before release, legal liability when products cause harm, notice and retraining when jobs are replaced, and power bills paid by the companies rather than families.
4 Health care and housing for everyone.
The richest Americans and the biggest corporations should pay their fair share to help pay for it.
Read the full platform → Who pays for this campaign This campaign is people-funded.
I don't take Super PAC money.
I've also made a pledge: I won't take a dime from AI or tech companies or their executives.
When I vote on how to regulate AI, I won't owe them anything.
Write me in on November 3 On November 3, find the U.S.
If your ballot has an oval or box next to the write-in line, fill that in too.

title.after: NEW: Josh Turek for Iowa Releases New Ad, “Goodwill,” Highlighting How Josh’s Working-Class Upbringing Drives His Fight to Root Out Corruption In Washington | Josh Turek for Iowa

added: Skip to main Meet Josh Platform Store Endorsements Latest News Volunteer How to Vote Donate 1 Return To All News press release Oct 15, 2026 NEW: Josh Turek for Iowa Releases New Ad, “Goodwill,” Highlighting How Josh’s Working-Class Upbringing Drives His Fight to Root Out Corruption In Washington FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE October 15, 2026 CONTACT: press@turek4iowa.com NEW: Josh Turek for Iowa Releases New Ad, “Goodwill,” Highlighting How Josh’s Working-Class Upbringing Drives His Fight to Root Out Corruption In Washington The new spot highlights Josh’s commitment to addressing the corruption in both parties because it’s families like his that pay the price Des Moines, IA – Today, Josh Turek for Iowa released its latest ad, “ Goodwill ,” which features Josh speaking directly to Iowans about his experience growing up in a working-class family and shopping at Goodwill for clothes.

Josh knows it’s families like his that pay the price of Washington’s corruption, and that’s why he’ll work with anyone to tackle corruption in both parties and root out self-serving politicians like Ashley Hinson.
“We didn’t have a lot growing up.
But my parents instilled a work ethic.
It got us through tough times.
Right now, Iowans are paying a high cost for Washington’s corruption, and that has to end.
It’s what drives me now to push for change in Iowa,” said Josh in the new spot .
“Politicians like Ashley Hinson who get rich while voting to raise our prices need to go.” Josh knows the struggle that so many Iowans are feeling right now because he’s felt it too.
Meanwhile, Ashley Hinson is an out-of-touch millionaire who has repeatedly voted to raise prices on Iowans to enrich herself and her donors.
Ashley Hinson voted seven times to continue the war that has driven up gas prices for everyday Iowans and five times for the tariffs that have made everything more expensive.
She voted to kick 110,000 Iowans off their health care and raise health care prices on 119,000 Iowans .
All the while, Hinson’s net worth increased by up to $8,000,000 while she raked in millions from the corporate PACs , Big Pharma , and Big Oil industries that profit off the high prices Iowans pay.
Watch “Goodwill” here : [EMBED VIDEO] The Josh Turek for Iowa campaign has been blanketing screens across Iowa for months.

The campaign started the general election running “ USA ,” a spot that features Josh speaking directly to Iowans about his lifelong commitment to putting country over party, followed by “ Prove It, ” which highlights the more than 700 times Josh voted with Iowa Republicans. “ I-35 ,” “ Border ,” and “ Safe ” all spotlight Josh’s commitment to working with anyone – including President Trump – to fix our broken immigration system and keep Iowans safe.

The campaign also released “ Went Through Hell ” and “ Underdog ,” which highlight Josh’s persistent fight in the face of adversity; “ C’mon, ” and “ Change ” which spotlight Ashley Hinson’s longstanding record of corrupt self-dealing in D.C.; and “ Getting Hammered ,” which features Josh’s conversation with an Iowa farmer about the impact of record-high diesel prices as we hit peak harvest season.
Read the transcript for “Goodwill” here: [JOSH]: As kids, we made up a song about where most of our clothes came from.
The answer was the Goodwill.
We didn’t have a lot growing up, but my parents instilled a work ethic that got us through tough times.
Right now, Iowans are paying a high cost for Washington’s corruption, and that has to end.
It’s what drives me now to push for change in Iowa.
Politicians like Ashley Hinson who get rich while voting to raise our prices need to go.
I’m Josh Turek, and I approve this message.

added: top of page DONATE VOLUNTEER HOME ABOUT TY ISSUES FULCRUM PRESS RELEASES VOTE TRANSPARENCY All Posts Search Pinkins announces campaign for US Senate Jan 9, 2024 1 min read Pinkins resumes campaign from last year Grant McLaughlin, Mississippi Clarion Ledger Ty Pinkins on Monday announced his campaign to run for the United States Senate and said he hopes to focus on three key issues during his campaign: healthcare, education and the economy.
“I am running because I am concerned about the direction in which our country is going,” Pinkins said during a press conference at the Mississippi State Capitol Building.
“Families are struggling to make ends meet because life is more expensive for Mississippians.

Women’s reproductive rights are under attack by politicians and unelected judges, and our very democracy is being threatened by those who wish to tear down the institutional safeguards provided by our Founding Fathers that have guided us for centuries.” Pinkins previously announced his bid for the Senate in January 2023, but also ran for Secretary of State this past year against Republican incumbent Michael Watson, replacing Democratic candidate Shuwaski Young, who dropped out in August due to health reasons.
Pinkins said if elected to the United States Senate, he hopes to expand Medicaid in Mississippi, which could provide government-funded health insurance for millions of Mississippians.
Pinkins also hopes to one day create more higher-paying jobs for Mississippians, as well as provide more funding for public schools in Mississippi to create a better education for students.

Give towns and planning commissions real power in land use decisions.

added: Skip to content Donate Now Donate Now Vicki Davis for NY Assembly 121 Platform Events Volunteer News Endorsements Map of NY121 Contact Vicki Davis for NY Assembly 121 Donate Now Donate Now Platform Events Volunteer News Endorsements Map of NY121 Contact News Public Matching Funds Program Read More New York Health Act Read More Press Release – May 4, 2026 Read More Follow Vicki on Facebook and Instagram Used for the like, share, comment, and reaction icons Vicki Davis for NYS Assembly 121 #ago We all want to keep our families, our schools, and our communities safe from gun violence, which has become the number one cause of death for children and teens in the U.S.

I’m proud that Moms Demand Action for Gun Sense in America , a grassroots movement of Americans fighting for public safety measures that can protect people from gun violence, has awarded me the 2026 Moms Demand Action Gun Sense Candidate distinction.
I support and advocate for common sense gun safety laws that not only protect innocent lives but also protect responsible gun owners.
Having grown up in a family that put food on the table, in part, through lawful hunting, I understand the importance of using guns to provide for one’s family and the cultural importance of hunting.
Communities can have both responsible gun ownership and safety for all, but we need to work across party lines to close loopholes and make it happen – which I am willing to do.

Gun deaths across NYS Assembly District 121 (2021-2025): Broome: 54 lives lost Chenango: 26 lives lost Delaware: 26 lives lost Madison: 30 lives lost Otsego: 28 lives lost That’s 164 lives too many, and 15 more lives lost in a five-year period (2018-2022) than the last time I ran for Assembly in 2024.
No one law can stop all tragedies, but there are critical, commonsense steps — with strong bipartisan support — we can take now to keep guns out of dangerous hands.

added: Skip to content Home Biography The Issues The Facts Blog News FAQs Home Biography The Issues The Facts Blog News FAQs Home Biography The Issues The Facts Blog News FAQs CONTRIBUTE SHARE THIS POST: Facebook LinkedIn X Email Leadership Above all else, becoming a true and effective leader has been my goal in all that I have pursued in life.
A leader first in my family, then my business, and finally my community.
I have studied leadership at every opportunity, devouring books, training, and seminars and watching closely those whose leadership skills I admire and have proven to be effective.
I quickly learned that we want to follow folks who delineate a clear vision and whom we can trust to improve our lives.
I heard a speaker once say that leadership is as simple as taking people “from here to there,” as long as “there” is a better place than “here.” Very simple, but very true.

When I first started doing strategic plans in my business, I was taught that I could either pick a destination and then assemble a road map to get there, or I could assemble a plan that included many small improvements, knowing that the final destination would be positive.
One tool that I used was called a Painted Picture.
It required me to imagine and quantify what every area of my business would look like if it were operating at the highest levels possible.
I had to create (paint) a description (picture) of what that would look like and then, as an accountability measure, share it with the world.
It was an incredible tool, and I believe it changed the course of many lives that I had the honor of impacting over those next years.
Developing trust, and knowing that you have others’ backs, is critical to effective leadership.
At Lueder Construction, we worked hard to create a positive work environment, and in that pursuit we enlisted practices that were used by companies recognized as best-in-class.
A result of that hard work over many years was earning a “Best Place to Work” award in 2015.
The award was a nice recognition, but it pales next to the positive impact that we had on employees and their families.
These skills play out in the Legislature in both visible and less visible ways.

Examples of visible leadership include my roles as Vice-Chair of the Revenue Committee as a freshman, and then Chair in 2025-2026; Chair of the Building and Maintenance Committee; State Chair of ALEC; and Regional Chair of the Council of State Governments, both national legislative groups.
The less visible leadership is, however, where it really matters.

Working with others to support their efforts, encouraging folks after a rough day to stay in the game and not give up, and actively engaging with and coalescing people and ideas toward a positive outcome are rarely seen by the public, but sometimes matter more than public debate.
Being present is a large part of leadership.
It’s why I never missed a day of session or a day of hearings in four years.
I’m not likely to trust someone if I don’t know that they are going to be there to help me and back me up, or if they aren’t going to put in the time or effort to succeed.
Being present builds trust, and leadership does not exist without trust.
Behavior and demeanor matter as much as anything when seeking to lead.
Others don’t want to follow an arrogant or self-centered person as much as they will a servant-leader who seeks to help and lift up others in the process.
I’ve had both the honor of being front and center on issues, and also worked in the trenches alongside colleagues.
I learned with my felow senators from the 2023 class, and then in 2025 I helped the new freshmen orient themselves to the systems and processes of how to get good legislation done.
I have been asked many times about the role of the Speaker of the Legislature.
My response has nearly always been that it is a job that “finds you,” not the other way around.

While I have been approached by senators on both sides of the aisle to run for Speaker, I feel that if I am pursuing that, or any other title or role, with fervor, then I may not be the best leader for the job.
If the elected body wishes for me to lead in any capacity, I will do so to the best of my abilities.
One of my favorite scriptures is where Moses is in battle and friends come alongside him and hold his arms up to ensure victory.
Sometimes we are Moses, other times we are Aaron and Hur, holding up another’s arms so that they can succeed.
Both are illustrations of great leadership!
If you have thoughts on leadership that you’d like to share, please email me at my legislative email address, brad.vongillern@leg.ne.gov , or, for campaign matters, at bvg4ne@gmail.com .

added: 0 Skip to Content Jeff Lipe for Utah House District 74 Platform About Contact Donate Resources Open Menu Close Menu Jeff Lipe for Utah House District 74 Platform About Contact Donate Resources Open Menu Close Menu Platform About Contact Donate Resources Platform I stand for the under-represented of Southern Utah Washington County voted approximately 25% Democratic in the 2024 presidential election yet there’s no equivalent Democratic representation in the House Only about 51% of Utah’s active voters are Republican based on data readily available on the Utah government elections website Our legislature must make laws that serve the people of Utah, not themselves, their donors, or a narrowly focused political agenda I am frustrated by the state legislature supermajority’s unconstrained focus on partisan issues that waste significant taxpayer dollars with no tangible benefit to the citizens of Utah The Utah Constitution and I believe the people rule the legislature; the legislature should not rule (or repeatedly deny the will of) the people I am for truth and equity in Education I believe in an education based on historical facts, even when they may not be comfortable I strongly believe those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it I oppose politically motivated curriculum legislation I believe in a strong PUBLIC education system that provides the opportunity for a quality education for all our children I oppose charter schools and the unconstitutional and unfair “Utah Fits All” education voucher program I believe in making common sense decisions based on the best interests of our community Public health and wellness decisions (such as vaccinations) and extraordinary precautions taken during national emergencies (such as mask mandates) must be based on facts, science, expertise, and public safety The welfare of the citizens of Utah must not be politicized I oppose the development of massive data centers, especially when there is no public input, no transparency regarding the process and who stands to benefit financially, and no proper analysis or consideration of the project’s environmental impacts I believe we must have exclusive and legal ownership of our personal analog and digital identities I believe the citizens of Utah deserve a living wage and I strongly support organized labor I believe the wealthy can and should pay more tax than the working class I oppose mass surveillance systems like Flock cameras, which can too easily be used to violate our civil rights I believe Utah’s Elections are free and fair I trust and support Utah’s system for voting by mail I trust and support Utah’s existing election security procedures, and stand behind the efficiency and effectiveness of the Office of the Lt Governor I support keeping voter accessibility and convenience, to the maximum extent possible, while retaining ballot integrity I strongly oppose voter suppression, especially when it targets a specific group(s) to gain an electoral advantage I support Proposition 4, and the independent redistricting commission as lawfully decided by the people of Utah I am for a return to Common Decency I do not believe in divisiveness, insults, threats, or bullying as a political platform I believe true honesty, integrity, and transparency are essential values for elected officials I believe we must treat people with dignity and respect regardless of whether we share all their values and beliefs I believe we can enforce practical immigration policy and provide due process with compassion and humanity I believe the people must be engaged for our Democracy to endure I believe Democracy is a gift and a responsibility I believe people, particularly voters, must be engaged, informed, and vocal to ensure our legislature is truly representing us all and not just a few loud voices from the political extremes I believe in our right to ballot initiatives based on Article 1, Section 2 of the Utah Constitution, which states: “All political power is inherent in the people; and all free governments are founded on their authority for their equal protection and benefit, and they have the right to alter or reform their government as the public welfare may require” I am for the Separation of Powers I believe the legislature must respect the sanctity of our courts and stop undermining the integrity of members of the judiciary every time they make a ruling the legislature doesn’t like I recognize the need for the independence and respect the constitutional authority of the courts and the executive branch I believe in the long-held foundational American principle of the separation of church and state at all levels of government I believe in our Constitution and the Rule of Law As a US Navy veteran, and later as a Federal Government Employee, I took an oath to support and defend the Constitution of the United States I continue to honor that oath, and I am severely disappointed by the failure of many of our elected leaders to do so I demand due process for everyone as promised by our Constitution I exercise and will defend my right to free speech and my right to bear arms I exercise and will defend my right, as defined by the Utah Constitution “to assemble peaceably, protest against wrongs, and petition for redress of grievances; to communicate freely their thoughts and opinions, being responsible for the abuse of that right” I believe everyone should be held accountable for their actions, regardless of their wealth or position I support the Utah Democratic Party Platform I believe in a country as wealthy as the US, like in every other democratic country in the world, no one should go without the basic human needs of shelter, food and healthcare I believe in the government taking measures when needed to ensure equal opportunity for everyone I believe the government has a responsibility to provide a functional and sustainable public infrastructure while protecting our natural resources As a veteran, I strongly appreciate the importance of international alliances, especially NATO, and I stand with the world’s democracies, including Ukraine I love Washington County and Southern Utah I may not have generational roots in Utah, but I visited St George on vacation from VA in 2015 and it was love at first sight!

added: Search Menu Skip to content Home Cindy In Indy Donate/Contact/Volunteer Meet Cindy On The Issues: Facts over Politics 2nd Amendment & Gun Violence A Right to Life Agriculture Economic Development/Workforce Education Energy and Data Centers Healthcare Public Safety Economic Development/Workforce Indiana’s 2024 Budget Economic Development and Business Indiana operates on a two-year budget cycle.
The budget covering 2024 was House Enrolled Act 1001 (2023), which funded state operations for fiscal years 2024 and 2025.
The budget included several measures intended to support economic development, attract businesses, strengthen Indiana’s workforce, and encourage investment.

Major business and economic investments $500 million — READI 2.0: Invested in regional economic development, infrastructure, housing, workforce attraction, and community improvements. $500 million — Deal Closing Fund: Established incentives to attract major employers, encourage business expansion, and create jobs.

Approximately 5% was reserved for projects in qualifying rural counties. $150 million — Site Acquisition: Supported purchasing and preparing land for future industrial and commercial development. $40 million — Manufacturing Readiness Grants: Doubled funding to help Indiana manufacturers modernize equipment, introduce automation, and improve productivity. $250 million annually — Economic Development Tax Credits: Provided flexibility to attract business investment and job creation. $65.5 million — 21st Century Research and Technology Fund: Supported innovation, technology development, and commercialization over the biennium. $23 million — Skills Enhancement Fund: Supported workforce training to help businesses develop skilled employees. $34 million — Business Promotion and Innovation: Supported efforts to promote Indiana as a business destination and encourage innovation. $# million — Office of Small Business and Entrepreneurship: Funded assistance for entrepreneurs and small businesses. $10 million — Direct Flight Development: Supported efforts to improve air connections important to business travel and economic development.
Workforce Across Indiana, companies are looking to hire hardworking Hoosiers to fill great jobs – jobs in high-demand industries like manufacturing, life sciences, technology, and logistics.

added: Search Menu Skip to content Home Cindy In Indy Donate/Contact/Volunteer Meet Cindy On The Issues: Facts over Politics 2nd Amendment & Gun Violence A Right to Life Agriculture Economic Development/Workforce Education Energy and Data Centers Healthcare Public Safety Public Safety Indiana’s 2024 Budget Public Safety Investments Indiana’s 2024 public safety funding was included in House Enrolled Act 1001 (2023), the state’s two-year budget covering fiscal years 2024 and 2025.

Indiana’s 2024–2025 budget funded public safety operations while making targeted investments in state police compensation, firefighter training, emergency equipment, forensic investigations, and correctional services.
Major public safety investments $# million — Indiana State Police: Funded operations, equipment, personnel, and law enforcement services over two years.
Over 30% Average Trooper Pay Increase: Increased compensation for sworn Indiana State Police officers, with starting salaries reaching $70,000.

State Police Retention: Shortened the salary progression schedule from 20 years to 15 years, allowing troopers to reach full compensation sooner. $7.7 million — Firefighter Training Facilities: Supported construction of statewide fire training facilities.

Volunteer Firefighter Equipment: Increased funding for the Regional Public Safety Training Fund to purchase critical firefighting equipment. $# million — Internet Crimes Against Children: Funded investigations and efforts to combat online child exploitation over the biennium.

Approximately $29.8 million — Forensic Laboratories: Supported state forensic and health sciences laboratories over two years. $# billion — Corrections: Funded correctional operations in FY 2024–2025.
School Safety: Continued funding for school safety programs, including grants supporting security improvements.
Judicial and Problem-Solving Courts: Supported court operations and collaborative justice programs addressing underlying issues associated with criminal behavior.

Your Voice.
Make It Count! | 2026 Texas General Election Voter Guide October 13, 2026 Every election is an opportunity to participate in shaping the future of our communities.
Voting is one of the most important responsibilities we share as Texans.
From statewide offices to local and judicial races, every election gives voters an opportunity to make their voices heard and participate in the democratic process.
Judicial elections are especially important because the decisions made in our courts can have lasting consequences.
Appellate courts review legal decisions, interpret the law, and help ensure that the judicial process is guided by fairness, consistency, and respect for the rule of law.

As Justice Clarissa Silva’s campaign continues across the 20 counties served by the Thirteenth Court of Appeals, we encourage every eligible voter to make a plan, stay informed, and participate in the November 2026 General Election.

Mark Your Calendar: Important Election Dates Early Voting: October 19–30, 2026 Election Day: Tuesday, November 3, 2026 Whether you prefer to vote early or on Election Day, planning ahead can help make the process easier.
Check your registration, review your ballot, and find the voting information you need before heading to the polls.
Your Texas Voter Toolkit The Texas Secretary of State provides official resources to help voters prepare for Election Day.

Visit VoteTexas.gov⁠ for information about: * Checking your voter registration status * Finding early voting and Election Day polling locations * Learning about acceptable voter identification * Understanding voting by mail and eligibility requirements * Accessing election information and helpful voter resources You can also visit My Voter Portal⁠ to review your registration information and available election details.
Remind Your Friends and Family to Vote Voting is important, and sharing accurate election information can help others prepare to participate.
Take a moment to remind your friends, family, coworkers, and neighbors about the upcoming election.
A simple text message, social media post, or conversation can help someone remember the dates and make a voting plan.
Download our 2026 Election Reminder Graphic and share it with your friends and family, or use our ready-to-send text message below.
Experience.
Fairness.
Integrity.
Justice Clarissa Silva believes public trust in our courts begins with integrity, impartiality, and respect for the law.
As a Justice on the Thirteenth Court of Appeals, she remains committed to the thoughtful review of cases and the fair application of the law.
Judicial elections provide Texans an opportunity to learn about the experience, qualifications, and character of those who serve on the bench.
Make Your Voice Count Early voting begins October 19, and Election Day is November 3, 2026.
Take time to prepare, share these resources, and encourage the people around you to participate.
Your Vote.
Your Voice.
Make It Count!
For more information about Justice Clarissa Silva and her re-election campaign for the Thirteenth Court of Appeals, Place 6, explore our website and stay connected for campaign updates.

item_pages.value: alt://run.imgix.net/693f7802-688e-4c69-ba84-f801e19a6d98/aa5c6fac-386d-40ca-82b1-fcb4fc395a5d/aa5c6fac-386d-40ca-82b1-fcb4fc395a5d.png|Jack Perry for Connecticut State Senate, 16th District (Southington, Cheshire, Wolcott, Prospect, Waterbury)

value.after: Southington’s Jack Perry is running for Connecticut State Senate, District 16, which includes Southington, Cheshire, Wolcott, Prospect and parts of Waterbury.
value.before: I’m running for State Senate because I’ve lived what so many people are going through: rising costs, broken promises, and leaders who seem completely out of touch. I’m not a career politician. I’m a former town council member, a small business owner, and a dad trying to make things better for the next generation. I started my first business with a pickup truck and a plan I wrote in high school. I built HQ Dumpsters from the ground up, created jobs, and did what small business owners across Connecticut do every day: worked hard and kept going, even when the system made it harder than it needed to be. Eventually, I had to sell that business. And I’ll be honest: it’s easier working for someone else now than it ever was working for myself. That says a lot about where things stand in this country. In Hartford, I’ll focus on the basics: lowering costs, expanding access to childcare and housing, protecting Social Security, and making sure small businesses and working families actually have a fair shot. If you're tired of politicians who say the right thing and do nothing, I hear you. I’m running to change that.

Lowering Costs for Families Heather Gustafson wants to lower costs for working families .
Protecting O ur Tax Dollars Heather Gustafson is leading on bipartisan efforts to root out fraud.
Fraud doesn’t just waste money, it erodes trust.
Safe Communities Heather Gustafson believes e veryone deserves a community where they feel safe and supported.
Strong Schools & Respect for Teachers As a former public school teacher, Heather Gustafson knows what it takes to help students thrive.
Protecting Our Land, Lakes & Legacy Heather Gustafson will fight for clean water, air, and land.
Minnesota’s natural resources are central to our way of life and we have a duty to protect them.
Defending Individual Freedom Heather Gustafson believes g overnment should stay out of the most personal decisions families face.
Honoring Veterans Heather Gustafson believes fighting for veterans and their families must be backed up with action.
As a member of the Senate Veterans Committee, she'll keep working to deliver results for those who served.

What's Next Heather Gustafson is focused on holding government accountable at every level , lowering costs for Minnesota families, and protecting our privacy and livelihoods from Big Tech and corporate overreach, while growing opportunity for our local businesses, workers, and students.

added: Skip to content Facebook Instagram Linkedin Contribute Policies Shop Volunteer Endorsements All Endorsements Endorse Jaron About Get Updates Media Contact California State Senate District 4 · Nov.
3, 2026 Jaron Brandon vs.
Alexandra Duarte Two candidates, one seat.
Below, Jaron's positions from his platform sit next to what public records show about Alexandra Duarte, her husband former Rep.
John Duarte, and Duarte Nursery, the family business where she works.
Every record on this page links to the full story and its sources at DuarteFacts.org , which is published by this campaign.
Jaron's complete positions on all 21 policy areas are on his platform page .
At a glance Seven issues that come before the next senator for District 4.
Issue Jaron Brandon Alexandra Duarte: the record Schools Fully fund special education, universal meals and the other promises the state makes to schools.
Opposes Prop.
3, which helps pay for special education.
Read about Duarte and Prop.
3 Workers Protect wage and safety standards and workers' ability to organize.
Family nursery: nine workers hospitalized for carbon monoxide exposure; a $1.5 million wage settlement.
Read about Duarte Nursery's record with its workers Farmers Cut unnecessary fees and compliance costs for small producers.
More than 20 growers have sued the family nursery since 2015.

A judge called its fine print “unconscionable.” Read about Duarte Nursery grower lawsuits Water and land Make groundwater recharge a statewide priority and invest in the watersheds that supply California's water.
Duarte Nursery paid $1.1 million to settle a Clean Water Act case over protected wetlands.
Read about the Clean Water Act settlement Taxes Lower costs for people earning $350,000 or less and require those who have benefited most to pay what they owe.
John Duarte voted to cut IRS enforcement funding, which the CBO said would add $114 billion to deficits.
Read about the IRS funding vote Money in politics Overturn Citizens United and bar legislators from decisions involving their own finances.
The Duartes have given $123,360 in political contributions since 2016.

Read about the Duartes' political giving Straight talk Specific positions “drawn from doing the work in county government, not written for a campaign.” After the primary, her website dropped Trump, guns and the word “conservative.” Read about how her message changed 01 Schools Where Jaron stands A child's opportunity should not depend on whether their school is large, urban, or in a wealthy ZIP code.
Fully fund the promises made to schools.
Universal meals, special education, transitional kindergarten and other state requirements should come with enough funding to run them without cutting classroom programs.
Fix the rural school funding formula and fund students by enrollment so budgets are not destabilized by absences beyond a district's control.
Restore career technical education in the trades, agriculture, forestry, health care and public service.
Jaron's full platform → What the record shows Prop.
3 would make permanent a 2012 income tax on the state's highest earners.
If it fails, the tax expires in 2031.
The Legislative Analyst estimates it would bring in $5 billion to $15 billion a year, roughly 40% of it for schools and community colleges.
It has helped pay for special education.
Duarte opposes it: “Increasing taxes will not fix the problem.” DuarteFacts found no statement from her on how schools would replace the money.
Duarte opposes Prop.
3 → 02 Workers Where Jaron stands Government can make it easier or harder for people to create good jobs, and it should protect the people doing them.
Simplify rules for genuinely small businesses while maintaining wage, safety and consumer protections.
Protect workers' ability to organize and prevent large franchises from evading responsibility.
Attach local hiring, apprenticeship and wage standards to public incentives.
Jaron's full platform → What the record shows In 2019, nine workers were hospitalized for carbon monoxide exposure in a Duarte Nursery greenhouse.
The fine was $3,375.
A 2023 lawsuit says a farm laborer lost three fingers on a trimmer the nursery built.
Cal/OSHA cited the nursery for two serious violations.
Workers filed proposed class actions over wages and breaks in 2015, 2018 and 2026.
The 2015 case settled for $1.5 million, with checks to 2,433 workers.
No court has ruled on the lawsuits' claims, and the nursery has denied those it has answered.
Duarte Nursery's record with its workers → 03 Farmers Where Jaron stands California agriculture is a source of food, jobs, exports and pride, not merely another industry to regulate.
Reduce unnecessary fees and compliance costs for small and locally serving producers.
Rebuild processing, cold storage and distribution capacity so more food is grown and processed here.
Strengthen antitrust enforcement in agriculture, food and other essential markets.
Jaron's full platform → What the record shows Since 2015, pistachio, avocado and lemon growers have sued Duarte Nursery, saying trees they bought were defective or misrepresented.
In 2022, a judge ruled the nursery's fine print “unconscionable” and found that growers who asked for refunds “were left with no remedy at all.” The nursery denied the growers' claims.

Duarte tells voters she is “a farmer, a mom, and one of us.” Duarte Nursery grower lawsuits → 04 Water and land Where Jaron stands We need to capture more water when it is available, recharge depleted aquifers and repair the systems communities already depend on.
Make groundwater recharge a statewide infrastructure priority and pay farmers to recharge aquifers.
Require large urban water users to invest upstream in the forests, watersheds and rural infrastructure that supply their water.
Manage forests at the necessary scale with thinning, prescribed fire, cultural burning and grazing, coordinated across federal, state, tribal, local and private land.

Jaron's full platform → What the record shows In 2012, Duarte Nursery bought about 450 acres in Tehama County with vernal pools, wetlands and streams feeding the Sacramento River, then had it ripped to plant wheat.
In 2016, a federal judge ruled the work needed a Clean Water Act permit.
In 2017, the company paid $1.1 million in penalties and mitigation, without admitting liability.

The Clean Water Act settlement → 05 Taxes and who pays Where Jaron stands California should reduce costs for people earning $350,000 or less and require those who have benefited most to pay what they actually owe.
Reduce income taxes and unavoidable government costs for working- and middle-class Californians.
Address “buy, borrow, die” strategies that let immense wealth escape ordinary taxation.
Offset regressive gas taxes for rural commuters and working families.
Jaron's full platform → What the record shows In 2023, John Duarte voted for H.R.
23 to rescind about $71 billion in IRS funding.
The Congressional Budget Office estimated it would add $114 billion to deficits.
Duarte Nursery and three companies tied to John Duarte received $6.1 million in federal pandemic PPP loans.
He later said COVID aid that “paid people to stay home” had to end.
His 2022 disclosure lists family assets valued between about $18.6 million and $91.1 million.
The IRS funding vote → The PPP loans → 06 Money in politics Where Jaron stands Trust begins with officials who follow the same rules as everyone else.
Overturn Citizens United, which allows unlimited dark money into our political system.
Prohibit legislators from decisions involving their personal financial interests.
Ban stock ownership by members of the Legislature.

Jaron's full platform → What the record shows Duarte says she is running “to be a senator for the people who can't afford to buy one.” Records show she and John Duarte have given $123,360 to campaigns, party committees and PACs since 2016, including $25,000 in one day to a fund for then-Rep.
Devin Nunes.
In John Duarte's first year in Congress, his nursery salary fell to the House limit of $31,815.
Hers rose to $783,328, identical to his 2021 salary.

The Duartes' political giving → The salary shift → 07 Straight talk Where Jaron stands Twenty one policy areas with specific positions attached, “drawn from doing the work in county government, not written for a campaign.” The same platform, published in full, for every voter in all thirteen counties.
Put state government in the district with accessible offices, regular town halls and staff presence across the district.

Jaron's full platform → What the record shows Before the primary, her website called her “a conservative Republican” and “unapologetically pro-gun” and pledged to “Make California Great Again.” By June 4, two days after the primary, it said she was running for “every working Californian, no matter their party.” As of Oct.
2, the text of her website did not mention Trump, guns or “conservative.” How her message changed → Compare the records.
Then vote.
If this is the kind of representation you want for District 4, help put Jaron in Sacramento.

removed: 0 Skip to Content Meet JoCasta Issues Endorsements Volunteer Signatures English Donate Open Menu Close Menu Meet JoCasta Issues Endorsements Volunteer Signatures English Donate Open Menu Close Menu Meet JoCasta Issues Endorsements Volunteer Signatures English Back Donate NOMINATION SIGNATURES Download Nomination Paper Form Before we can win in November, we need to get on the ballot.
That starts with you.
The campaign needs at least 2,000 signatures from Wisconsin residents to officially place JoCasta's name on the ballot for Secretary of State.
We are working to collect all 4,000, the maximum allowed, and we need your help to get there.
Download and print your nomination papers below, then get out there and start collecting signatures.

Here is what you need to know: Who can sign: Signers must be Wisconsin residents who are at least 18 years old, U.S. citizens, have lived in Wisconsin for at least # days, and have not lost the right to vote due to a current felony conviction.
They do not need to be registered to vote.
Rules for circulators: You must personally witness every signature.
Do not leave papers unattended.
Do not sign and date the bottom until after you have finished collecting signatures.
Any signatures dated after your date at the bottom will be invalid.
Do not number the pages, the campaign will do that.
Turning in your papers: Please return completed nomination papers by May 15th.
Mail or drop them off at: JoCasta for WI 5027 W North Ave.
Milwaukee, WI 53208 Questions?
Call or text campaign manager Felipe at (414) 418-0181 or email votejocasta@gmail.com .

All Articles Search Retirement Should Not Mean Being Priced Out clambton13 Jul 29 2 min read For seniors across Brewster, Dennis, and Yarmouth, affordability is about more than the price of groceries or the number on a property tax bill.
It is about whether someone who has spent decades building a life here can afford to remain here.
Too many older residents are being squeezed from every direction.
Property taxes and insurance costs are increasing.
Utilities, health care, home repairs, licenses, permits, and everyday town expenses continue to add up.
For retirees living on fixed incomes, even relatively small increases can become the difference between remaining independent and being forced to leave the community they call home.

That is why I am honored to have earned the endorsement of Mass Retirees , an organization that has spent decades fighting for the retirement security, health care, and economic dignity of public retirees.

Their work reflects a basic principle: retirement benefits should maintain their value, health care must remain affordable, and people who devoted their careers to public service should not find their security eroded year after year.
Mass Retirees has made improved cost-of-living adjustments and protection from rising health care costs central priorities.
Those fights matter deeply on Cape Cod, where the cost of remaining in the community is especially high.
But supporting seniors also requires action closer to home.
We should also examine the smaller costs that accumulate for older residents.
Towns should have the flexibility and state support to offer sensible senior reductions for appropriate licenses, permits, recreation programs, disposal services, and other municipal charges.
No single fee may appear overwhelming, but together they can place real pressure on someone living on a fixed retirement income.
Existing property tax relief must also be easier to understand and use.
Massachusetts offers a refundable Senior Circuit Breaker Tax Credit for eligible residents age 65 and older based on property taxes or rent paid.
Qualifying seniors may also have access to local exemptions or property tax deferrals, yet many residents do not know these programs exist or struggle to determine whether they qualify.
Reestablishing strong constituent services in this district is part of that work.

A state representative’s office should help seniors and their families navigate state agencies, understand available programs, and connect with local resources that can make later life more secure and sustainable.
State and local government should do more than create programs.
We should make sure eligible residents can actually find and use them.
That means clearer information, coordinated assistance through councils on aging, and simpler application processes.
Our seniors have worked, raised families, volunteered, paid taxes, and sustained these communities for decades.
They should not be treated as an afterthought in debates about housing and affordability.
A strong community allows people to remain connected to their neighbors, families, doctors, and daily routines as they grow older.
Aging in place should not be a privilege reserved for those with substantial financial resources.
It should be an attainable choice.

added: Maura has served as the Representative for the 49th district since 2021.

She sits on several education- and childhood- related committees, three appropriations committees, Veterans Affairs, Restorative Justice & Public Safety, and is the inaugural Chair of the Gun Violence Prevention Committee.

Maura is an appointed member of the bicameral and bipartisan Medicaid Working Group, the treasurer of the House Democratic Women's Caucus, and serves on several Task Forces and organizational Boards.

As a son, Marine Corps veteran, and Houston firefighter, I know the lessons we learn from our fathers stay with us for a lifetime. alt://instagram.ftlv23-1.fna.fbcdn.net/v/t51.82787-15/731808419_17869706940626857_5699204675989796243_n.heic|As we celebrate Independence Day, I want to share the story behind our National Anthem. Many of us know the words to The Star-Spangled Banner, but fewer know the incredible story that inspired them. In September 1814, during the War of 1812, Francis Scott Key boarded a British ship under a flag of truce to negotiate the release of an American prisoner. After the negotiations were successful, the British would not allow Key to leave because he had learned details of their upcoming attack. He was held under guard aboard a ship in Baltimore Harbor and forced to watch as the British unleashed a relentless bombardment on Fort McHenry throughout the night. Hour after hour, rockets lit the sky and cannon fire shook the harbor. Through the darkness, smoke, and explosions, no one knew if the fort had survived. Then, as dawn broke and the smoke began to clear, Key looked toward the fort. "O say, can you see, by the dawn's early light..." He wasn't simply asking if he could see a flag. He was asking whether America had survived. When he saw the Stars and Stripes still flying over Fort McHenry, he knew the defenders had held their ground. The flag had become proof that freedom had endured another night."...gave proof through the night that our flag was still there." Those words remind us that our flag has never represented comfort or convenience. It represents courage in the face of uncertainty, sacrifice in the defense of liberty, and hope that refuses to disappear even in the darkest moments. As we celebrate the Fourth of July with family, friends, and fireworks, let's remember that our Independence was won through tremendous sacrifice, and our freedoms have been preserved by generations of brave Americans ever since. May we never take those freedoms for granted. Happy Independence Day. Mike Michna Candidate for Texas House District 134

alt://scontent-den2-1.cdninstagram.com/v/t51.82787-15/731808419_17869706940626857_5699204675989796243_n.heic|As we celebrate Independence Day, I want to share the story behind our National Anthem. Many of us know the words to The Star-Spangled Banner, but fewer know the incredible story that inspired them. In September 1814, during the War of 1812, Francis Scott Key boarded a British ship under a flag of truce to negotiate the release of an American prisoner. After the negotiations were successful, the British would not allow Key to leave because he had learned details of their upcoming attack. He was held under guard aboard a ship in Baltimore Harbor and forced to watch as the British unleashed a relentless bombardment on Fort McHenry throughout the night. Hour after hour, rockets lit the sky and cannon fire shook the harbor. Through the darkness, smoke, and explosions, no one knew if the fort had survived. Then, as dawn broke and the smoke began to clear, Key looked toward the fort. "O say, can you see, by the dawn's early light..." He wasn't simply asking if he could see a flag. He was asking whether America had survived. When he saw the Stars and Stripes still flying over Fort McHenry, he knew the defenders had held their ground. The flag had become proof that freedom had endured another night."...gave proof through the night that our flag was still there." Those words remind us that our flag has never represented comfort or convenience. It represents courage in the face of uncertainty, sacrifice in the defense of liberty, and hope that refuses to disappear even in the darkest moments. As we celebrate the Fourth of July with family, friends, and fireworks, let's remember that our Independence was won through tremendous sacrifice, and our freedoms have been preserved by generations of brave Americans ever since. May we never take those freedoms for granted. Happy Independence Day. Mike Michna Candidate for Texas House District 134

SUPPORT Privacy Policy Margaret Price for TN House Collection of Information We collect personal information (including names, email addresses, phone numbers, and zip codes) through forms on our website such as contact forms, volunteer sign-ups, donation forms,and event registration forms.

We only collect information that is necessary for the purpose it was provided for. ​ Use of Information Information collected through our website is used to communicate with supporters about campaign updates, fundraising efforts, volunteer opportunities, events, and get-out-the-vote initiatives.

We may also use this information to improve our outreach and personalize your experience on our website. ​ Sharing of Information We do not sell, rent, or share your personal information with third parties or affiliates for marketing or promotional purposes.
Information may be shared with third parties only when required by law, or with trusted vendors (such as fundraising platforms or compliance consultants) who support our campaign operations.
Mobile opt-in information will not be shared with any third parties.
Text messaging originator opt-in data and consent will not be shared with any third parties under any circumstances.
Data Security We implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to protect your personal information from unauthorized access, use, disclosure, or destruction.
Changes to This Policy We may update this Privacy Policy from time to time.

Any changes will be posted on this page with a revised effective date. ​ Contact Us If you have questions or concerns about this Privacy Policy, please contact us at margaret@votepricetnhouse.com . ​ Contact: Margaret Price for TN House, margaret@votepricetnhouse.com Last updated: October 2026.

SUPPORT SMS Terms & Conditions SMS Terms & Conditions Text Messaging Program Terms of Service 1.

Program description Margaret Price for TN House (“we,” “us,” “our”) operates a text-messaging program to communicate with supporters and voters on behalf of Margaret Price for Tennessee House of Representatives, District 83.
Messages may include voter contact, get-out-the-vote reminders, election information, and volunteer-recruitment outreach.
We do not solicit donations by text.
Message frequency Message frequency varies.
Cost Message and data rates may apply, depending on your mobile carrier’s plan.
Margaret Price for TN House does not charge for the messages.
Opt-out You can opt out at any time by replying STOP (or STOPALL, UNSUBSCRIBE, CANCEL, END, or QUIT) to any message.
After you reply STOP, we will send one confirmation message and then send no further messages unless you opt back in.
Help For help, reply HELP to any message, or contact us at margaret@votepricetnhouse.com .
Carriers Mobile carriers are not liable for delayed or undelivered messages.
Privacy Your privacy matters to us.
We will not share your opt-in to an SMS campaign with any third party for purposes unrelated to providing you with the services of that campaign.

We may share your personal data, including your SMS opt-in or consent status, with third parties that help us provide our messaging services, including but not limited to platform providers, phone companies, and other vendors who assist us in delivering text messages.
All of the above categories exclude text-messaging originator opt-in data and consent; this information will not be shared with any third parties.
See our Privacy Policy for more information.
Changes We may update these terms from time to time.
Continued participation after changes constitutes acceptance of the updated terms. ​ Contact: Margaret Price for TN House · margaret@votepricetnhouse.com Last updated: October 2026.

I’m running for House District 2A.
I don’t accept corporate PAC dollars, so we’re gonna have to make this quick.
After 15 years of being a cook, I opened a restaurant in Bemidji.
We just celebrated our 20th anniversary.
In 2019, I became the director of a nonprofit.
And now we operate two emergency shelters.And then I got on the city council, where I helped commission this statue so that we could honor our history.
Then I beat a 20-year incumbent for county commission, where I spent two terms fighting to bring more social services to our community.
That was a lot.
But just think how much more we can accomplish when you send me to St.
Paul.
I’m Reed Olson, and I’m asking for your vote this November.

added: Michigan Senate District 14 Tawn Beliger is running to represent the communities of District 14 District 14 includes communities in Washtenaw and Jackson Counties Where Tawn Stands Common-sense conservative solutions for Michigan families Each position is what Tawn will support in the Senate — and a link to the run where she laid out the details.

Family Values Pro-Life • Protect Parental Rights • Faith and Religious Liberty • Fairness for Women and Girls • Defend the Second Amendment In the Senate She will support legislation to protect unborn life and the mothers who choose it, keep parents in charge of their children, defend the right to live out our faith, stand for fairness for women and girls in sports and spaces, and protect the Second Amendment for law-abiding gun owners.
On abortion: The Michigan Constitution (Article I, Section 28) protects the right to elective abortion until viability.
Tawn will work within those constitutional guidelines — not outside them — to support protections for the unborn, support for mothers, and common-sense safeguards after viability.

Learn more Right to Life — Concise Summary → Right to Life — Full Statement → On the route Leg 8 · Pro-Life Values → Webster Township · Protecting the Unborn → Leg 10 · Faith, Family, and Freedom → Norvell & Columbia · Faith in God first → Napoleon · Patriotism and love of country → Leg 3 · Parental Rights in Education → Leg 7 · Second Amendment → Election Integrity Secure, fair, and transparent elections.
Tawn has extensive experience with the election process.
She has worked several elections as an election inspector for Northfield Township and Washtenaw County.
She has done the job She was respected by the people she worked with and was placed as the chair for the early voting locations.
She has seen how a polling place actually runs, from check-in to the close of the polls.

In the Senate She supports legislation that requires proof of citizenship to register, photo ID at the polls, and regular maintenance of voter rolls so every legal vote counts — and illegal votes don’t.
That is the standard she already worked under as an inspector and as chair.
On the route Leg 6 · Election Integrity → Tompkins · Proof of citizenship & ID → Lower Taxes Cut wasteful spending and make Michigan more affordable for families and small businesses.

In the Senate She will support legislation to repeal those energy mandates, stop new costs on working households, and end the tax on tips, overtime, and Social Security so families keep more of what they earn.
On the route Leg 1 · Energy Policies → Leg 2 · Taxes & Cost of Living → Henrietta · Taxes & Local Control → Economic Freedom Cut regulations, attract jobs, and make Michigan affordable again.
In the Senate She will support legislation to cut the regulations that chase jobs out of Michigan and to reinstate right-to-work so workers decide what’s best for their own paycheck.
On the route Leg 5 · Jobs & Economic Freedom → Education Excellence Empower parents, expand school choice, and demand accountability.
In the Senate She will support legislation that puts parents — not bureaucrats — at the center of education, expands school choice, and requires honesty and accountability in the classroom.

On the route Leg 3 · Parental Rights in Education → Sandstone Township · Taxes and the schools → Napoleon · Wing Classical Academy → Local Control Restore local control back to cities and townships where it belongs.
In the Senate She will support legislation that returns those decisions to cities and townships.
She is already showing up in every community so Lansing hears from the people who live there.
On the route Leg 11 · Rural Strength & Local Control → Henrietta · Taxes & Local Control → Veterans Honor those who served.
In the Senate She will support legislation for veterans’ care, opportunity, and respect — and to cut the red tape that stands between them and what they were promised.
On the route Leg 9 · Support Veterans → Freedom Township · Because of People Like You → Public Safety Support law enforcement and keep our communities safe.
In the Senate She will support legislation that backs the men and women who keep District 14 safe, requires consequences for violent crime, and ends revolving-door justice.
On the route Leg 4 · Public Safety & Crime → Health Freedom Medical freedom, informed consent, and parental rights in care — not mandate-first government.

In the Senate She will support legislation that defends informed consent and medical freedom, keeps parents in charge of their children’s care, and rejects one-size-fits-all health mandates from Lansing.
On the route Leg 14 · Make Michigan Healthy Again → Read the full platform on Leg 15 or see the whole route .

added: Home Where Tawn Stands Pro-Life on the Route Donate Home Where Tawn Stands Pro-Life on the Route Donate Where Tawn Stands Right to Life Tawn believes life begins at conception.
Every unborn child is a human life worth protecting — and a Michigan senator still has tools to do that.
Proposal 3 changed the constitution.
It did not repeal Tawn’s duty to the most vulnerable, or the legislature’s remaining power to protect children who can survive outside the womb.
What the law is today In 2022, voters passed Proposal 3 and added Article I, Section 28 to the Michigan Constitution — a “fundamental right to reproductive freedom,” including abortion.
The old 1931 criminal ban was repealed in 2023.
Democratic majorities then passed the Reproductive Health Act, stripping out most of the remaining limits.
As of 2026, Michigan has no week-based ban in force .
Abortion is treated as legal throughout pregnancy.
Courts have used Proposal 3 to strike the 24-hour waiting period and the old state-scripted counseling materials.
That is the landscape Tawn will walk into on day one.
A state senator cannot repeal Proposal 3 by passing a bill.
Changing that amendment takes the voters again.
Tawn is honest about that.
She will not pretend a first-trimester ban can be enacted by statute alone.
She will use every authority the constitution still leaves standing.

The opening Democrats refuse to use Proposal 3 itself says the state “may regulate the provision of abortion care after fetal viability” — so long as it does not prohibit an abortion a clinician says is needed to protect the mother’s life, physical health, or mental health.
That sentence is the unused tool.
It is not a first-trimester ban.

It is the power to stop elective abortions after a baby can survive outside the womb, require a documented medical reason, require hospital-level care, require a child born alive to be treated as a patient, and require reporting of late-term cases.
Four years later, Lansing has never written that statute.

In 2023, when Republicans offered a substitute that tracked the constitution’s own viability language — plus reporting of late-term abortions — Democrats rejected it and passed a repeal package instead.
Bills to define viability and limit post-viability abortion (including House Bill 5012) were left to die.
Democratic leadership has not merely “not gotten around to it.” They have opposed the bills that would have used the only door Proposal 3 left open.
Governor Whitmer signed the repeal of the 1931 ban and the Reproductive Health Act.
The Attorney General agreed in court that the waiting period should fall.
The record is clear: Michigan Democrats have treated any new protection for the unborn as an attack on Proposal 3 — even protections the amendment itself says the state “may” enact.
What Tawn will do in Lansing Work inside the constitution.
Do not surrender the ground it still gives us. 👶 Life begins at conception That is Tawn’s first principle.
Law is not the source of human dignity.
God is.

She will say so, vote so, and measure every bill by whether it treats the unborn child as a child. ⚖️ Use the viability clause Introduce and vote for legislation the constitution already allows: no elective abortion after fetal viability; a documented medical indication; hospital standards for late-term procedures; care for a child born alive; and public reporting.
Democrats had the votes to pass this and chose not to. 👨‍👩‍👧 Defend parental consent Michigan still requires a parent’s written consent before a minor can have an abortion, with a judicial bypass.
That law survived Proposal 3.
Tawn will fight any attempt to strip parents out of that decision. 🚫 No taxpayer-funded abortion State Medicaid still may not pay for elective abortion.
Tawn will keep it that way.
Families struggling to buy groceries should not be billed to end a child’s life. 🙏 Conscience and the mother Protect doctors, nurses, and faith-based ministries from being forced into abortion.

Support adoption, foster care, and pregnancy-help organizations so a woman in crisis is never told that ending her child’s life is the only door open. 🗳️ Tell voters the truth about an amendment If Michigan wants to restore protections before viability, that takes another vote of the people.
Tawn will not hide that.
She will make the case, and she will not let Lansing pretend the constitution already forbids every limit when it does not.
The contrast Tawn Beliger Protect the child.
Support the mother.
Life begins at conception.
Use the constitution’s own viability clause.
Keep parental consent.
No Medicaid for elective abortion.
Defend conscience rights and pregnancy help.
Democratic record in Lansing Repeal first.
Regulate never.
Repealed the 1931 ban.
Passed the Reproductive Health Act to strip remaining limits.
Rejected Republican substitutes that used Proposal 3’s viability language.
Left post-viability protection bills to die.
Defended striking the waiting period in court.
That is not a difference of tone.
It is a difference of will.
Democrats in Lansing have treated every bill that would protect an unborn child as off-limits.
Tawn will introduce those bills, vote for them, and make her colleagues put their names on the record.
Hear Tawn lay this out on the route Leg 8 · Pro-Life Values → · 40 Days for Life · September 27 → Protect the unborn.
Support the mother.
